en: The introduction to the commentary by the supremely compassionate Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai, titled *Arulicceyta Vyākhyānam*: "May the Lord, who is the Consort of Śrī, whose sole nature is knowledge and bliss, who consists of all auspicious qualities, who is endowed with both types of glory, and who is the Supreme Lord higher than all—may we behold Him through the eye of knowledge that has taken the form of devotion! Thus they pray. May He, who dwells upon their heads, graciously grant them the vision for which they long, even though they themselves have not yet attained it. May He, who is ever-present before them, bestow His grace so that they may indeed behold Him. Thus he speaks.

They pray that they may experience the realization of virtues even in the supreme state, by means of the eye of wisdom, within the temple that is filled with the inner virtues such as ethical conduct (*śīla*).

What is this experience? What is prayer? To this: by the grace of the Lord who has bestowed freedom upon us, and because there are others who would restrain us as humans, we must strive to ensure that those who have attained this experience do not fall into the pits of their own families; and likewise, we must pray, as our Ālvār did, that "this Tamil may remain for ten thousand years. Those who wish to experience this must practice accordingly. Like pearls strung together on a thread, they shall shine brightly.
This very same body, which was formerly called the thousand-eyed Indra,
the sun, the great earth, or the infinite,
now sports with its belly as white as a conch shell.
In the city of Tiruvaraṅkapuram,
on the banks of the golden river,
I have built a temple with pillars of precious gems, soft as the touch of a maiden’s hand. Thus I declare.

Regarding the phrase "kaṇ iṇaikaḷ" (these very ones), the *Paryaṅkavidyā*—beginning with "iruliriya" and so forth—describes the longing of the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*). Desiring to experience [the Lord] within that body which has emerged from the chest of the venerable Anantāḷvān and is seated upon His lap, they long for Him. In the passage beginning with "pāde nādhyārohati" (he ascends onto the feet), regarding the statement "who are you? made by the one who has entered the couch (*paryaṅka*) shining with great splendor, he replies, "I am a prince," and says, "I am Brahman."
The jewels that shine upon his hood, which are as radiant as the sun and moon, and the thousand hoods themselves— each one possessing a brilliance that rivals the light of ten million suns—
shine forth.

Furthermore, he possesses a thousand hoods that have attained the status of the sacred Tiruvaṭi (the divine lotus), and he is the great serpent king known as Aravāra Ca Perum Cōti, endowed with supreme splendor.

To the Lord of All, who dwells pervading me and all other things, and who is called "Ananta" (the Infinite) because His own essential nature and attributes are infinite— I bow to that very same Tiru Anantālvān, who, having assumed the form of a serpent with a thousand hoods, manifests the proximity to the Blessed One inherent in those among them known as Sumukha, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others, and who, by means of his lower body coiled around the base of the mountain, supports this entire world.

Even if one were to say, "Vaikuṇṭha exists in that other world beyond the great city of Tiruvaraṅkapuram," they would see it right here: in this very great city of Tiruvaraṅkam, there flows the Kāverī, whose waters are as clear as oil and whose banks are golden; and on its banks stands the temple where the sacred sandals rest. There, the sage Kaṇva beheld the Lord who was graciously looking upon him—a sapphire set within the jeweled crown of the Lord Anantāḻvān.

Having embraced me, whose tenderness was as delicate as a fresh sprout, and having embraced me, who am like a young elephant, where have you gone? Where are those arms that once rested upon my chest? Where are those words? Where are those glances? Where are those smiles? Where are those playful gestures? Where are those tender embraces? Where are those sweet words? Where are those glances? If one were to count the days spent thus, and if one were to count the times one has said "I am food, I am food, I am food," would it be possible to count them?
Even if the ocean were to dry up and the earth were to split asunder, the end of those [countless] hundreds of thousands of years would not be reached.
Thus spoke the Goddess.
Even if one were to wash away the impurities with the waters of the Vitāna river,
they would only spread further;
yet, the impurity of that person’s own body is like a flower that sheds its scent.
On the day when he was born, crying out,
"My heart is pierced by the arrows of love for the one who sits upon the lotus-throne of his hips," he wept for six days.

The wind has brought a hundred thousand auspicious breezes from the shore of Yaśodā’s house, where Kṛṣṇa’s touch resides; it has come to provide the nourishment for my happiness through the excellence of the joy of experiencing the Lord. May the wind also bring a thousandfold nourishment for the love born from that supreme bliss. Let these winds blow—winds that purify the hymns and other songs of praise.

He who dwells in the sky, which is as vast as the ocean and shines with the splendor of the firmament, he who is invincible and possesses a power that overwhelms all adversaries—he is the venerable Anantārya.

Even as the flowers of the forest fade away, he alone remains fresh; though the world may perish, he alone does not wither. With the brilliance of the flames of fire that flicker within him, he alone shines forth.
He who wears the garland of the *pū* flower upon his sacred head—what other garland can compare to the *pū* flower?
What other garland can equal the *pū* flower? To the Lord of All, who dwells within the garland fashioned from those very *pū* flowers, I bow.

In the temple that stands firm within the city of Araṅkattāravāṇai on the Kaṭi river, where the glorious Lord Anantāḻvāṉ dwells, I have been awakened by the grace of the Lord who manifests through the sage Kaṇva. With my mind fixed upon that wondrous being who graces us through Kaṇva, I stand with two pillars of joy; with great exultation, I stand with two pillars of rapture.
"Come along! he called out, and though I ran for a day and a night, there was no end to it; he kept running on and on, and I kept giving him this food.
Even now, as I think of that man, my two eyes have become swollen with tears.
Having gathered the bees that had come from the forest and placed them upon her mother’s face, she sat there, her own lotus-like face blooming like a golden lily.
Even in the midst of the wheel of worldly existence, which is without beginning or end, they playfully sport with their own mother;
for how many days have they not cried out, "O Mother, O Mother!"?
For how many days indeed!

Furthermore, this person is Brahmā, born from the lotus that emerged from the navel of Viṣṇu. That is to say—it is said that he alone is capable of composing hymns and the like, and that even if others were to compose them, they would not equal those hymns;
thus, it is said that the four Vedas, which serve as the retinue for the hymns and so forth, exist solely by virtue of his faith. This is what is meant.
Taking hold of the face of the eastern direction, and taking hold of the four faces that shine upon the four Vedas— having established the eyes,
the ears, the nostrils, and the rows of teeth up to the lips,
as well as the eyelashes, for the sake of experiencing the world, they provide the necessary means for every single moment of perception.
To that one who, moved by love, stands with palms joined in reverence and recites hymns and other praises;
to that beautiful Mother who emerges from her own lotus-like navel—the source of all things, including this desirable world and its entire causal realm—and who shines forth like a radiant lotus bud.

In this world, which is like a forest of thorns, even while dwelling in the temple that serves as an ornament to the cycle of existence—specifically in the temple of Tiru Anantāḷvāṉ where Lord Sarveśvara graces us with His presence—the people of Aṇi, Araṅkattāravāṇai, and Paḷḷikoḷḷu gather at the foot of His sacred tree. They bring flowers and other offerings, and day after day they perform circumambulation. Do they not say, "We too shall become like them"? And do they not also say, "We too shall perform circumambulation"? Thus, [the verse begins] with "The circumambulators of the lineage," and so forth.
The fragrance of the jasmine blossoms that have bloomed this morning enters my ears; having risen early this morning,
I am filled with longing for the one who has come.
The immortal sages sang of him as the one who protects the Tamil land;
the ancient seers praised him as the one who dwells within the heart-lotus of those who have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
"O my mother, you have become a boat for me who am drowning;
O my father, you have become a garland of flowers for me who am scorched by the heat"—thus crying out, they weep day and night.

May those who, though themselves distressed, effortlessly cause the distress of their dependents to vanish—those who are bewildered by their own dependents, thinking "we are the ones who must protect those who oppose us"—[may they be blessed].

If one were to describe the time, it would be a period of conflict for those who have taken refuge [in the Lord]; if one were to describe the place, it is the mountain that stands firm against the torrential rain of Indra during the rainy season—a mountain that has come to me as a refuge from the fierce heat of the summer.
This mountain, which removes my fatigue, is my refuge. As for the people:

there are those who are like a rogue who has lost his way, wandering about with disheveled hair; there are those who, though they claim to be noble, are actually base; and there are those who, having encountered a teacher who has come to them, do not rise to greet him. These are the people who have come to me. As for the water: it is the water that removes my exhaustion. It is this water that is my refuge.
To him who, out of compassion, protected those who were helpless and lacked both livelihood and the memory of past favors;
to him who, having taken upon himself the burden of his own existence, bore the children of others as his own;
to that Lord, whom the immortals seek to attain through their own efforts; to that eternal Sun, who dwells in equality with all, even while bearing the weight of the world—[I bow].

To the Lord who dwells in the temple where the Tamil *Iṉpa Pāviṉai* shines, where the pearls of the *Cuṭar Maṇi* are strung together; to Him who came forth from the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇam* as the *Vaṭa Moḷi*; to the Lord who, having heard the *Paṟṟu Araṅkattār* verses at the time of the *Arav’aṇai* festival, granted His own presence to those who had come to the *Paḷḷikoḷḷum*; to the Lord who, in that temple where the eternal residents dwell for no other purpose, graciously appeared to the *Kaṇvaḷar* upon the *Tiruanantāḷvān-mēl*.
Having composed hymns with such intensity that they seem to rise from the depths of the ocean of my heart, my kinsmen ask, "Why do you weep?

And when I offer my hands joined in *añjali* with flowers and other ritual implements held so tightly they seem to burst from the palms of my hands, they ask, "Is there no joy here? Why do you grieve? To this, I say: "It is not that there is no joy; it is because I am unable to bear this [suffering]."
"Neither Tumpuru nor Nārataṉ knows how much there is;
though they have weighed the *tol* of the *marai-nūl*, they cannot say how many *tol* of dust particles there are. Thus it was said.
In the city of Aravaṇai,
where the flower-sellers sell jasmine garlands,
I saw Maṇivaṇṇan embracing his mother at the temple gate.

On the day when the forest-dwelling sages cried out, "The Mālava flower has blossomed," there was no other wealth; on that day, the incomparable Tumburu and Nārada, having reached this shore of the world, sang hymns while dancing amidst the flowers of the sacred feet. Tumburu and Nārada, who had arrived at the shore of this shoreless world, danced and offered praises within the sacred precincts.
The Vedas and Shastras,

which are like the cotton-wool of the scales, cannot weigh even a single speck of dust compared to the hymns of praise; for Brahma, who dwells within the lotus of the sacred navel, having offered prostration at the Lord’s feet, composed this hymn,
while the jewel-adorned celestial nymphs sang of His sovereignty and His other divine glories.

In the great temple of Araṅkattāravaṇai, which is like a palace for the vast intellect of the Sage (Maṇikkavācakar), I shall bathe in the sacred waters of the Anantāḻvān tank; having bathed in the Maṇivaṇṇam tank, I shall embrace the Mother; and having embraced Sarveśvara, who dwells in the forest of Aḻakki, I shall say, "I have smelled your flower," and on that day, while I am walking in the forest, may he place his hand upon my head, saying, "I am weary. Thus shall I walk in the forest within his sacred presence.

The bees, mistaking it for a lotus amidst the filth, swarm around it; the gods, thinking it to be a celestial tree, gather there; the sages, perceiving its true nature through their wisdom, know it as such; and the bees, repeatedly smelling the fragrance within the filth, mistake it for a lotus and, having entered the foul-smelling mire, even the swans and the lotus-eyed ones are deceived.
The Brahmā who dwells within the lotus that blooms from the navel of Viṣṇu—

who is said to have emerged from the ocean of milk after churning it with Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vāsuki as the rope— and his son Rudra, along with Indra, who studied together with them;
these three gods, together with their lineage of immortals and the host of deities who attend upon them, all dwell there.

The great sages, from Arampaiyar down to Rambhā among the Apsarases, as well as Sanaka and the others, all meditated upon Him with their minds absorbed; yet, though they sought Him through the contemplation of Brahman,
not one among them could describe Him even by a single word.

In the *ticai* and *ticaiyil* [sections], having caused all the flowers that bloom in the spring to fall as a rain of blossoms, he [Śiva] brought forth the jasmine flowers that bloom in the summer; then, in the autumn when the lotuses bloom, he brought forth the water-lilies that bloom in the winter. Thus, upon the body of the Lord Anantāḷvāṉ, the Kaṇvaḷar, the Kaṭal-vaṇṇar, and the Kamalakkaṇṇar—the water-lilies of the winter—began to bloom.

Having embraced the divine face of the one who dwells in the sacred forest, he sang the praises of the moon rising over the mountain; yet, having embraced the divine face of the one who dwells in the sacred forest, how could I not weep, crying out, "Where is he?"—my heart sinking as I wander through the forest day after day, thinking, "How shall I find him?
Even though my mind knows the truth, it wanders like a deer lost in the woods.
The aims and goals have been cast aside;
they run about crying out, "There is no more food!
There is not even a blade of grass to eat; the world has become a wasteland where nothing grows.
In the golden city of Aruṅgattāraṇai, where the three-fold path meets the mind, he dwells; and in the three-fold path of Nīram,
he is the one who has swallowed the serpents of Māyōṉai.
On the day when one realizes that the mind is like a stone that sinks in water, one must understand that the mind possesses three qualities:
hardness, weight, and density. Because of these, the mind, emerging from its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), sinks and perishes as it goes along.

Having set aside the aims of this world and the pleasures of the next, having built a firm bridge across the ocean of worldly existence, and having crossed over the shoreless misery that arises from the suffering of the world,
one should practice the five-fold daily rites (pañcakāla) with the thought, "I am the slave of the Lord," and "I am the slave of the Great Lord. In these times, one should practice thus.

In the village of Araṅkāttu on the banks of the Ponnī river, within the sacred boundaries of the forest where the *toṇṭar* (forest-dwellers) lived according to their ancient traditions, there resided a community of Vaiṣṇavas who were devoted to the Lord and whose minds were primarily characterized by compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*). For them, the Supreme Being was the highest goal to be attained;

thus, while they performed their daily rites at the temple on the banks of the Ponnī, they also worshipped the Lord in the form of the Tiru Anantāḷvān image located within the golden *araṅkattu*. It was there that the Kaṇva sages received His grace.
Is it on the day when, having seen the temple— which serves as an ornament for the playful manifestation of the golden mountain,
Mount Aruṇācala— and having seen that wondrous being who dwells within it,
my eyes shed tears; or is it on the day when, seeing the beauty of his face, I embrace him and my eyes flow with tears of bliss?
If one does not know the four Vedas after learning them,
one will suffer the punishment of being tied to a pillar and having one's head shaved; likewise,
if one knows the Vedas but does not practice them, they say that person is a mere beast.
Having crossed the bitter sea and reached the city,
he entered the sacred temple at Tiruvarankadu, which stands upon the banks of the river Cūḷkāppa, amidst the groves of mango trees and the fragrant breezes of spring.
"Is this a garland worn around the neck?
"No, it is a bow.

Thus they spoke, and on that day, the Śrīśārṅga bow—which had been hidden within the sacred sandals—was brought forth. When the people asked, "Will he carry it on his shoulder?", the elders, knowing that there was indeed a bow, placed the Śrīśārṅga upon the shoulders of the sacred sandals and carried it for twenty steps.
When the Lord was experiencing His bliss within the Kūṉ Nal Caṅkam, He took up the Śrīpāñcajanya conch and blew it twice;

as the sound emerged from that experience, it struck the opposing side with such force that they were crushed like a handful of sand thrown into a fire, and the weapon remained fixed in their bodies like a stone embedded in a tree. Thus spoke Tiru Āḷiyāḻvān.

The one who possesses the *koṟṟam* (the power of movement) is the Lord who manifests supreme sovereignty, the *Tirukoṟṟavāḷ*. Regarding *koṟṟam*: it means "to move. It refers to the power of movement that exists with such speed as to cause one to wonder whether the mountain is moving, or whether the earth is moving, or whether the wind is moving; it is the power of movement that exists within the Great Mountain (*Periyatiruvaṭi*) itself. This is the power of movement that exists within the mountain.

Having thus entered the city, Cūḷkāppa Rāmalakṣmaṇagupta, along with Ennumāpōlē Kaṭaṟkarai Veḷiyilē Śrīsenai, all of whom were his kinsmen, as well as Tampi and Tampiyār, and Kākkumāpōlē, remained stationed at Periyatiruvaṭi, from the boundary of Periyaperumāḷ Kaṇvaḷarnt until the arrival of the grace of the Lord, while the Śrīpañcāyudhāḷvār waited there, ready to strike.

In the sacred city of Tiruvaraṅkaṭṭu, within the temple that stands upon the banks of the river flowing through Cōlai-cūḻam, he embraced Sarvādhikān—who was filled with unsurpassed bliss after hearing the words of the sage Kaṇvaḷar spoken from the mouth of the Lord Anantāḻvān in the temple that shines like the Cōlas and the Kalas who dwell there—while his own body was covered in the ashes of the sacred ash (celārnta) and his hair was matted (mālōṇai), and he remained immersed in the divine nectar (celālē) of the sacred teachings. He held him close, having heard the words of the supreme one as they issued from the lips of the sage.

Even if one were to say, "I shall go," and after passing away from this world, one were to have to search for that Reality which remains present here, would it not be a great sin for me to experience such difficulty? Indeed, everything that stands as an obstacle to the experience of the Lord is nothing but sin.
Therefore, quickly, with a focused mind, recite even a single verse of the Tiruppukaḷ.
Far away from the mind’s impurity, with ears alert like a mountain that steals the clouds,
he roams the vast forest; for even a single day,
he has donned the bark garment and stands firm upon the heights of the mountain.
In the city of Tiruvaraṅkattāravāṇai,
having climbed the palace tower and gazed upon the Mother’s face,
he sang praises and danced for six days.

Even if worldly people were to experience the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, for many days—just as one might say, "The mind has been quickly struck by the blows of the sword"—and even if their sense organs were to reach a state of complete satisfaction, the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, who remain at a distance even for a moment from the experience of the Lord, would read the *Tiruppukal* verses from the *Kulañjāṭi* and recite the *Tirunāma* verses which express His auspicious qualities. They would do so even while eating the food offered to Him (*avaṉuṭaiya*). Even for them, these [worldly experiences] would be like a mere trifle. Thus, even if they were to enjoy the objects of the senses for many days, the sense organs would not find fulfillment; yet, for those Śrīvaiṣṇavas who dwell far from the experience of the Lord, even the reading of the *Tiruppukal* and the *Tirunāma* verses would bring them great joy. Therefore, even if one were to experience the objects of the senses for many days, the sense organs would not attain satisfaction. But for the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, who remain far from the experience of the Lord, even the reading of the *Tiruppukal* verses from the *Kulañjāṭi* and the recitation of the *Tirunāma* verses that proclaim His auspicious attributes would suffice. Even while consuming the food offered to Him, they would recite these verses. For them, [the worldly experience] would be like a small thing. Thus, even if they were to experience the objects of the senses for many days, the sense organs would not reach a state of satiety. Having cast aside the great wealth of the world, having cast aside the gods,
having cast aside jewels, and having cast aside those who act with compassion,
there is not even one among them who does not tremble at the sound of the drum.
Having cast off the burden of sin,
the weariness of the world, and the smallness of the body, they have entered the temple; may the arrows of the Lord of Tirumūrttattāṭiyār strike them down.
On the day when he rose from his sleep after having slept for a great length of time,
saying, "I am hungry," the gods rose up,

as did the great wind, and the worlds situated above the world of Brahmā, including the realm of Brahmā and others, rose up from the calamity of the occasional dissolution (*naimittikapralaya*); and having restored life to those who were there, such as Brahmā and the rest, the Lord of the Temple dwelt within the temple in the world of Brahmā.

Having cast off the pride of mind and having cast off the conceit of the heart, Śrī Vibhīṣaṇāḻvār sang: "By means of this [grace] which shines forth as the very life-breath, may the earth, the sentient beings upon the earth, and the sins that cause one to suffer incessant, unbearable, and immeasurable suffering—sins that never cease even for a moment—be entirely removed;
and may there be an unending happiness that is never mixed with suffering."

The Śrīvaiṣṇavas—who were filled with unsurpassed bliss through their experience of the Lord, who had manifested as the fish, the tortoise, and the boar—departed from that place and went to Tirumūrttam. There, they offered the kingdom to Śrī Vibhīṣaṇāḻvār, the son of Aṇi Araṅkan, and departed. In the presence of Periya Perumāḷ, who was pleased by this, Aṇi Araṅkan established his own residence within the sacred precincts (Tirumūrttam) of that very temple. He made that very spot his dwelling place.

Having heard the words of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas—who dwell in great palaces, who are filled with unsurpassed bliss, and who have mastered the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*—if someone were to say, "I am an anointed Kṣatriya," would you not say, "He is one among them"? On the day he comes seeking me, saying, "I am your servant; I am your ruler," and while he is waiting, do you not serve him by attending to his pleasure, as if he were a Śrīvaiṣṇava?
In the golden hall of Tiruvarankattaravanai,
where the tiger leaps and the lion roars,
even the earth itself trembles; O Mother, you who are the refuge of all, protect me.
The one who,

having made the earth a mere trifle, caused the ocean to overflow its shores, and who, by his own power, brought the city of Kaṇāra to ruin— was he not the king Kulacēkaraṉ, who ruled over the Col country?
The actor Vilangu Tamil, the garland-maker Pattum Vallar,
the carpenter Nalam, the mason Tikal Narana,
and the weaver Nanuvārē— these six, having fashioned the sacred image of Vilangu, brought forth both the face and the hands; and Kāvēri, flowing from the mountain peak, brought forth the feet.

In the city of Tiruvaraṅkattāravāṇai, where the Mother Goddess herself dwells in the palace of the mountain, Lord Sarveśvara—who removes all fatigue—resides within the temple of His own Mother, seated upon the lap of the Infinite Consort (Anantāḷvān).
May He, who is ever gracious to those who seek Him, grant me the experience of His presence through my ears and throat, as I sing this song of praise. Thus ends the Ācaippāṭṭu.

The Lord granted his grace so that the fort might not perish, even though the fort of Veṅkoṭṭakūṭai— along with its towers, ramparts, moats, and gateways, as well as the army that protected it and the elephants that displayed its majesty— was being besieged by the Kulacēkaras of Koṭai,
who were acting as executors of the will of the Chola king.

To those who wish to compose Tamil verses that are as captivating as a dramatic performance, and who desire to master the art of poetic expression through the proper arrangement of words, there are those who have come here to offer instruction. They are the disciples of Periyaperumāḷ, who resides at Tiruvaṭikaliṉ-Kīḷ; he is one who possesses the qualities of character such as virtue and compassion, who is the lord of all, and who is a king of affection. Come and experience his presence! Thus spoke the elders.

In one who has attained the state of being an object of the Blessed One, there exist certain innate dispositions: the resolve for conformity (*ānukūlya-saṅkalpa*) and so forth. These are: the resolve for conformity, the avoidance of opposition (*prātikūlya-varjana*), and the desire to protect through conformity. Conformity consists in being an object of the Blessed One and being an object of the devotee of the Blessed One (*bhāgavata*). There is no obstacle whatsoever for one who desires to possess such conformity toward the Blessed One in its entirety.

Thinking, "There is no obstacle whatsoever," he spoke thus to those who desired his word: "I shall give my own body as a gift to this excellent substance; I shall offer my own body as a gift to him who has prepared the *tirumañcanam*; I shall offer my own body as a gift to him who has prepared the *amṛta* (nectar); and I shall even offer my own body as a gift to him who has prepared the *allātam*. Let them take it from me. In this way, there was indeed no obstacle for him at all, for he possessed complete mastery over every subject.

By means of the knowledge found in such passages as "The man of wisdom is My very self" (*jñānī tvātmaiva me mataṃ*), "The Pāṇḍavas are indeed My life-breaths" (*mama prāṇā hi pāṇḍavāḥ*), and "He is My very own" (*pattar āvi*), there arises a favorable attitude toward his [the devotee's] object [of devotion], while a contrary attitude arises toward the object of the Lord. By this knowledge, it is understood that both of them—[the devotee and the Lord]—are one and the same. The favorable attitude arising toward the object of the Lord is shown in the *Tirumoḷi*; the contrary attitude arising toward His object [the devotee] is taught in this *Tirumoḷi*.
Then, the flower-gatherers, having gathered flowers for the sacred Mother, the daughter of the mountain,
who dwells upon the southern slopes of the Tirunelveli hills, and having fashioned garlands for Mārvaṉ, the lord of the forest, they sang songs of praise;
and as they danced with great joy, the Lord of the Flower-Arrows (Kāma) struck them with his arrows.

Thus, when the multitude of those who have sought refuge at his feet has gathered, the introductory section (*avatārikai*)—beginning with "those [who are] such" (*teṭṭarum*) and so forth—sets forth the subject matter concerning the *Bhāgavata*, intending to describe those who have plunged into the qualities of the Lord. By taking refuge in Him as the Master of the Field (*kṣetramuṭaiyaṉ*) and the Master of the Meaning (*arthamuṭaiyaṉ*), they become His intimate associates (*bhagavad-pratyāsatti*). Thus, this work speaks of them.

Having composed a hymn concerning the Lord, he then composed a hymn concerning the Teacher, saying to them: "In the matter of the Lord, there is knowledge and devotion; [he is] 'the mass of knowledge and detachment.
Even that is easily attained by him who, having given his own effort, has seen the truth;
for he is the one who, having given himself, gives even the power required for the constant experience of Him—He who is the giver of self and the giver of strength. Thus he spoke.

Having established his eternal residence in Tiruvaraṅkam—the city so desirable that people say, "I would rather be a beggar there"—he remained for some time. One day, while he was walking along the street, he saw a woman selling jasmine garlands. He purchased a garland from her and, placing it upon his head, offered auspicious blessings for their mutual welfare. Then, with hearts full of devotion, the devotees sang songs of praise.
Thinking it their duty, those who were devoted to him as if he were their own father embraced him with affection; yet,
though they had prepared themselves for his funeral rites,
they could not bear to see him depart according to that succession, for he was one whose sole purpose was devotion to another and who was subject to the will of others.
Thus: "From now on, we shall go to the forest; let us see the noble families of the elders.
When they had thus gathered, he said: "What purpose is there for me in seeing them? There is no need for this at all. This is merely a visible purpose (to deceive).
With our feet covered in mud from the village streets, we shall appear as if we have come from afar by way of the forest path."
Thinking, "Let me not die; let me live," he gazes upon this world with longing, yet he does not see it as it truly is.
He who has come here, having cast off his name and his body, shall drink the water of the Kaṅkai tree and attain liberation.
Thus spoke the Lord.

The great-grandfather, the venerable elder brother of the Lord who dwells in Vāsasthāna, whose feet are washed by the waters of the Tāmraparṇī flowing from the mountain where the impurities of the world are wiped away, has also washed his two sacred feet with the waters of the Tōṭalām;
he has gone forth to experience them as they rest upon the broad white sands of his own shore, even as he cries out in joy at the sight of the waves breaking against the shore.

He struck down the demons who had gathered to devour him, and he shattered the seven walls that were exceedingly strong and possessed of infinite magic. He stood as the protector of those who take refuge in him, providing them with all kinds of arts and crafts. Having measured out the earth, he stood there and, placing a blade of grass in his hand, measured out the sky.
Thinking thus, and reflecting upon virtues such as his character, she did not perceive any other purpose for her life than him;
and because he remained ever with her through the intensity of her love, she would call out the sacred name of the Lord, crying, "O my husband!
and would even die by drowning herself in the well.

It is better to immerse oneself in the dust of the feet of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, who are pierced by the virtues of the Lord, than to wander through the forests of Toṇṭar, Aṭi, Poṭi, and Āṭa; for even a single connection with the Lord is obtained only through the dust of the feet of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, who have become sacred fords (*tīrtha*) by the grace of their masters.

"Is there any purpose in my coming here, like a crow crying 'water' when there is no water, or like a dog barking at a temporary connection, or like the Ganges flowing into a puddle on a dung heap? "Nala, Tikaḻcaṭaiyān," and so forth—let them go and say such things.
Whether they come to seize this land, or whether Rāma comes and kills me, or whether they split the mountain and pour down molten gold, let it be. I shall remain.
The ear-nectar that flows from the mouth of the Lord of the temple, who has adorned his body with the sacred marks, is sweet;
even the sages, who have tasted it, say it is exceedingly sweet.
And the hair of the bull, which serves as a pillow for the Goddess when she lies down in close embrace with him, is also exceedingly sweet.

If anyone should obstruct the acquisition of this land by Sri Bhumi Piratti, or oppose her in her efforts to annex it, I shall cause that person’s land to be submerged in the deluge; furthermore, I shall punish him with the heat of the sun and rain, and he shall be cast into the depths of the cosmic egg by Mahavaraha, who emerged from the earth and dwelt within it—just as Rama formerly slew Vali and cast him down into the nether regions. Thus shall I ensure that the land belongs to Piratti for all time to come.

When the great Bali, who was hostile to Indra, fled from the earth—having been pursued by the Lord of the Gods who had emerged from the mountain peak where the Kāverī flows with its waters as yellow as gold, having drunk the water of the Kaṇṇīrai that flows through the Vellama land, and having crossed the impassable forests and mountains—he entered the forest of Maṇalāntatu; there, the Pāṇṭiya king, seeing him, seized him with a firm grip that obstructed his union with his beloved, and having bound him, he brought him back to the city of Madurai, singing of these heroic exploits with overflowing affection. Thus, having captured him, he brought him to the presence of the King of the Pāṇṭiyas.

Having performed the *tiruppāṇi* for the sake of the sacred food (*tiruvalaku*) at the temple of Araṅkaṉ Kōyil, those who had offered it were about to depart with their mothers and kin when they encountered those who were crying out, "We have come! It was as if a great calamity had befallen them. Seeing the fault of being adorned with oil mixed with many inauspicious substances, they sought refuge in the feet of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, who were there for the sake of auspiciousness. Even though water, grass, curd, ghee, milk, and honey were available, they did not touch them, but instead went seeking [the Vaiṣṇavas]. *(Note: The passage describes a group of people who, having participated in a ritual at a temple, encounter others who are distressed by the presence of impure substances like oil and refuse common offerings, instead seeking the protection of the Śrīvaiṣṇava community.)*

My mind is weary, and my body is exhausted from wandering through the forest of delusion. O Lord, how shall I survive? My heart is consumed by the fire of grief. How shall I live? My mind is utterly distressed.

Having taken the water and curd that had been boiled with sugar-cane juice and added sugar, and having mixed the water and curd that had been boiled with jaggery, if there were even a drop or a particle remaining, those who drank it would become immortal within a short time; yet the ocean, seeing this, grew angry. There may be a limit to the affection of the rivers and the sea, but there can be no limit to their anger.
Having taken [the food] and having placed it in his hand, he ate it;
having placed it in his hand, he made him eat it.

O people, how can one who has eaten [this] know the suffering of others? Having bound me—who am like a substance possessing the touch of those who have sought refuge—by means of this [food], they have made me their own, as one who is not to be shared by another.

The Āṭiyārkaḷ (the teachers) who were present at the time of his incarnation said to him, "Come here; you shall easily obtain the grace of Periya Perumāḷ. Having thus spoken, they placed him upon a raft made of *eḻuti* wood and set it adrift on the river.
He cried out, "I am sinking! I am sinking!
and as he was about to drown, he called out his mother's name, "Amma! and remembered the Lord’s sacred name. Thus, he crossed over.

Having offered prostrations with their heads touching the ground, let all those who have come here stand with their heads bowed. Having gathered together those who are present here, having measured out this village,
and having set aside a portion for the temple expenses, let them remain within the mind, free from worldly objects, filled with unsurpassed bliss— the Śrīvaiṣṇavas at the feet of Śrī [Rāmānuja].

My heart says: "May they, who have come to this village as beggars, be satisfied with the butter-thievery they have committed. My heart says: "May they, who have been satisfied with that, give me back the milk they took. My heart says:
"May they, having composed a hymn saying, 'May these people of this village become our lords,' grant me the blessing: 'May this [butter] be yours forever.
Who is he that, having gathered the fallen leaves and spread them out, has gone away, crying "Aravīrtta"? Who is he? (40)
If this mind of mine, which has crossed over the ocean of worldly existence, were to perish, then my heart would surely perish;
for it is my heart that grieves when those who have attained the state of the Lord of the South (Śiva) pass away.
May my heart not perish.

Then, Kāliyaṉ—who had been polluting the water by pouring out poison while the fish and turtles were drinking from the tank at Tiruvāyppāṭi—suddenly leaped up with a roar as if ready for battle, and having emerged from the pond, he became the lord and protector for all those present at Tiruvāyppāṭi.

The mind that has crossed over the three-fold ocean of worldly existence is like a small leaf; it is the mind that seeks to overcome others through mere cleverness. But the divine mind, which casts aside both the "three" and the "one," dwells in the temple of the body where the sages reside, speaking sweet words with a voice as resonant as the sound of a rain-cloud. What is this cloud? It is the cloud that has gathered from the mountain of the body, rising up from the earth. That indeed is what I call the cloud.

The Śrīvaiṣṇavas— who, having heard that the Daṇḍaka forest was shining with one thousand temples, went there thinking it was the city of Māṇikya-kūppi, and who, upon seeing the great Perumāḷs [deities] manifesting within their hearts as if they were the very essence of the mountain, experienced horripilation as they searched for the path while remaining in a state of intense spiritual rapture—
[are described here].

My heart yearns to experience that Great Lord (Periyaperumāḷ) whom they describe; having experienced Him, may I attain their state, and having attained theirs, may my mind attain His. All tangible substances are perceived, yet He is the formless substance.
Those who have seen Him—the Infinite, the Endless, the Unborn—have washed away the impurities of their sins and have entered the abode of the Pure Ones.
Having crossed over this ocean of worldly existence, having reached the further shore, and having become one who has transcended all suffering—
O Lord,
you who are the cause of the universe, my heart yearns for you even as it yearns for water in the desert.
He who exists even at the end of the dissolution (pralaya) in a state of being; he who exists as a single pervasiveness both in the causal state and the effected state;

he who exists as a wonder, appearing as if he were looking upon the various worlds that exist within his own belly, while remaining present in them as their very substance even during the state of effectuation—such is He.

He who exists as the sole sovereign over all those who are born, whether they be gods or men—He who is the Lord of the eternal goddesses, the Lord of both realms (the manifest and the unmanifest)—one must perform one’s duty by remaining steadfast in devotion, so that the dust of His sacred feet may not fall upon one’s head, and so that the lotus of His beautiful face may bloom within one’s heart. There is no other way.

My heart yearns to compose verses for the feet of the Great Lord (Periya Perumāḷ), who is worthy of exclusive devotion; yet my mind thinks that even if I were to compose verses for the Śrīvaiṣṇavas who possess devotion toward those feet, it would be like playing a flute for them after many births have passed—something they do not need. How can I, who am like a lowly worm in this city, ever hope to cross over the ocean of worldly existence? I shall sing of Him who wears the moon as His crest-jewel.
O Lord, you who are my refuge, you who are compassionate toward me—having heard that a great festival was being held at Aruṅgaṉ, my heart yearned for it;
and when I saw the crowds of people coming from all directions, my mind was filled with longing, thinking, "When will this time come?
O Lord, grant that this moment may arrive.

The Lord, who is the ornament of the lineage of those who speak the truth like a city-gem, and who possesses a beautiful divine smile that shines with the luster of a pearl necklace—He, along with His Consort, has come to this place; may He look upon us with favor.

May He also look upon the rows of teeth that shine like pearls extending to the ends of the lips, and upon the lovely redness on His divine lower lip, which is the supreme excellence of all this. May the Lord likewise look upon us.

Having offered the *āmpaṭi* (betel leaf) that reveals His glory, saying, "O Lord, You who dwell in the great abode, You who are the Great Lord of the city," and having offered the *hārattai* (betel nut) from the *vēṇumpaṭi* (areca nut garden), he said: "O Lord, You who dwell in the sacred city of Tirumāliruñcōlai, You who are the Great Lord renowned in both realms of manifestation, You who are of the nature of infinite splendor, the peerless One—may my devotion, which has been growing for a long time, become firm and endure until the end. Thus he spoke with deep affection.

To those who, with eyes fixed upon the ears of the one who is praised by the gods, gaze at Him with unsurpassed devotion, and who, out of the intensity of their devotion, even disregard their own bodies—my heart yearns that they may come to the sacred feet of Him for even a single moment; my heart dwells there, having no other purpose, dwelling in that state where there is nothing else.
May He, who wears a garland of forest flowers, grant me His grace again and again.
The garland-wearing Perumāḷ Tirumārvaṉ, who wears flowers upon his ears;
the garland-wearing Lord who dwells within the heart-lotus of those who have crossed over the ocean of existence;

the garland-wearing One who is the very essence of the world; the garland-wearing One who is the refuge for those who have fallen into the pit of worldly life—my heart yearns for that garland-wearing Lord.

The one who, upon the mere touch of his own hand, caused the jasmine garland worn by Kaṭal Kiṭanta-vaṉ to bloom like a cluster of flowers in the Tiruppāṟkaṭal garden, and who, out of compassion, granted the garland to Kaṇvaḷar; the one who, having accepted the great and sacred Mārvaṉai garland offered by Vaṇṭu Kiṇṭu Naṟum Tuḻāy, wore it as a fragrant garland on his neck; the one who, for the sake of Uṭaiya-varai—who dwells near the great and sacred Mārvaṉai garland—accepted the garland offered by Mai-pōl Neṭum Varaivāy and placed it upon his chest; that one, who is my sole refuge, dwells within me.

Having offered the lotus-like ears of the impure one as a flower-offering to the Lord who dwells within the heart, and having offered the impure sacred thread as a garland to the Lord who dwells within the heart, let the impure tongue recite the names of the Lord who dwells within the heart; and with devotion, let the impure body move about as a servant to the Lord who dwells within the heart. Let the impure mind wander about, impelled by love for Him.

To the Lord who dwells in the temple on the banks of the Tontarvāl river, where garlands are strewn for Him who is easily accessible; to the Great Perumāḷ, whom I have come to seek out, I offer my devotion. May the Śrīvaiṣṇavas and their Vaiṣṇava Lakṣmīs likewise offer garlands to Him—this is my heart’s resolve.
Having spoken thus, she went forth, gathering flowers that fell from the trees along the path.
Having thus lost his wealth and fallen into poverty, he wandered about crying out, "I am my own master, I am my own master!
His relatives, seeing him in such a state, said to him, "He is our father;
indeed, he is our father. But others replied, "He is not our father; he is the father of those others. Thus they disputed among themselves over whether he was their father or not.

Introduction—Let us proceed with the recitation. What is bile? It is that which causes burning. Regarding this subject: some say that bile and others are distinct from bile. Having stolen two pieces of gold from the hand of a merchant, they fled by way of Varṣadhārā;
their bodies were covered in horripilation as they ran away like deer.

Having stepped forward with this very foot and struck the ground, he leaped upward; having reached the height of the palm trees, he descended, and with that same foot he struck the earth again. Having stepped forward with this very foot, he stood relaxed; yet in that very place he stood motionless. Even though he did not move from that spot, he struck the ground with that foot and performed a frantic dance, and having reached the height of the palm trees, he offered a long prostration.
My own father, my grandfather, my master, my lord,

my elder brother, my maternal uncles, and those who are Śrīvaiṣṇavas who abide solely for the sake of Lord Periya-Perumāḷ— my maternal uncles, their sons, and the sons of those others, as well as those who are devoted to them and those who perform acts of devotion toward them,
are all my maternal uncles.

The Marraiyars were indeed *pittars*; those who perform this devotional practice are *pittars*, and those who do not are also *pittars*. Those who remain here performing this rite are Sanaka and the other [Ādi-siddhas], and they too are *pittars*. There, the impurities of the body, the flesh, the blood, and the marrow—all these impurities they pour out into the fire; thinking thus, one should meditate.

Kolli Kāvalan, Kūṭal Nāyakan, Kōḷi Kōn, Kulacēkaran, Collil, the Tamil Mālai, Vallavar, Toṇṭar, and Toṇṭarkal—where are they? There is no one there; it is only I, Maṅkai Nātan, the beloved consort of Śriyaḥpati Periyaperumāḷ.
The venerable elders [taught] that Śrīvaiṣṇavas, who exist with no other purpose than Him, are like a pair of sandals to His feet;
and they established me in the state of being His slave, according to that single moment of grace.

Kollikāvalan Kūṭal Nāyakan, who was the protector of both Kolligum and Maturaikkum, [was] the Perumāḷ known as Nāyakarān of Uraiyyūr. Regarding the verse beginning with "The great son-in-law, having fallen from his status, lived in the forest" (*periyavuṭaiyāruṭaiya iḻavāl vanta veṟuppālē*, *vanavāso mahodayaḥ*), although he had fallen from his kingdom and lived in the forest according to that verse, everything—including his falling from the kingdom and his dwelling in the forest—became a source of prosperity for him. Thus, even his misfortunes became a blessing for him.

To those who say, "I must go to the city of Ūṉērūcelvattūṭal," and "I must go to this Araccum," he grants them both their respective births—namely, birth as a *rāja* and birth as a *taṉṉai*—in accordance with their status as his *śeṣas*.

Having spoken thus, those who desire to attain the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—which extends up to the state of being the *bhāgavata-śeṣa*—are those who, by means of the words contained within this Tamil garland, have entered the Tamil land (*toṭai*) of the Vallavas and are themselves Vallavas, each according to their own measure. They are those who have reached the state of being the *śeṣa* of the Bhāgavata.

In the *Avatārikai*: "The Lord, having come forth from afar, dwelt for a long time in the great city," thus [it is said]; and in the *Kīḻil Tirumoḷi*, it is stated that even though there was no one else who could endure the intense longing for the Blessed One—extending even to the realization of being His *śeṣa* (servant)—He nevertheless appeared.

Thinking, "How many such people have perished in this world," and "How many such men have passed away," and thinking, "I too shall become like them," one should remain in a state of constant alertness through devotion to the Lord; for it is sufficient merely to form the resolve to do so. One should act by following the example of those who have already attained Him, and one should dwell in a state free from all that is adverse.

The scripture which states that the attributes of the Blessed One and His divine manifestations (*vibhūti*) are to be experienced as being of His nature (*tadīyatva*) must itself be abandoned. While the effects of knowledge (*jñāna-kārya*) manifest His purpose, the effects of ignorance (*ajñāna-kārya*) arise from dwelling together with a state in which the quality of darkness (*tamas*) predominates.

In his former state, the venerable Śrī Prahlāda, possessing the common notion that "I am everything," had said, "Of my father"; yet when he was about to be killed by those who acted with hostility toward the one who protects him, he saw him and cried out.

Having heard the beneficial words of Śrī Vibhīṣaṇālvāṉ Āntaṉ, [Rāvaṇa] remained in a state of distress for his own welfare; yet, as he was about to depart after taking him [Vibhīṣaṇa], thinking that by taking him he would not face adversity and would instead prevail, he took him and set out.

Let there be hostility toward [the following]: the state of identifying the body with the Self, the tendency toward sense objects, and the inclination to claim that there exists some other reality distinct from the body and the Self. To those who remain in such states, this Tirumoli says: "I have no need for you; I am enough unto myself. Just as one does not seek water for water already in the hand, I have no need to grasp you, O Lord, who are my very own.
You alone are sufficient for me.
"I am not a man of rank," he said, "I am one who has lost his wife and wanders about.

To him, my mother spoke of the path of liberation (*mokṣa*) and the path of worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), as well as the lack of inherent value in all things and the true value that exists within them. She explained how one may attain realization regarding the eternal reality of the Self (*ātman*) which exists within that which lacks inherent value, and how one may attain realization regarding the path of liberation that exists within the path of worldly enjoyment. Thus she spoke: "One should transcend *prakṛti* (primordial nature) through the enjoyments derived from *prakṛti*."
There is no one who would not wish to embrace me; there is no one among those who live with the conceit that the body is the self who would not say, "I am yours.
When you said, "Father," and so forth, you were declaring that there is another, distinct from the body and its like.
Indeed, you alone are the kinsman free of all conditions.
I thought to myself that it would be easy for me to go to the temple along with my mother, who had been suffering until the very end of her life, and to bring her back;
so I dug a pit and began to bury her.
As I was digging, my mother caught hold of me, saying, "My son," and after she had told me what he had done to her, I too buried him.
"There is no need for you to worry about whether this man will come or not;
whether he is a friend or an enemy,
let him come as he pleases," she said.
I am one who has never seen or touched a woman;

having heard of their beauty from others, my mind remains fixed on that beauty described by them. Women appear before me only in the descriptions of others. Even when I touch a single limb with my hand, I withdraw it immediately upon touching another limb.

There is no possibility of my ever seeing her face-to-face. For me, there is no connection whatsoever with those who dwell upon objects already attained, nor with those who dwell upon objects yet unattained.

Regarding the verse beginning with *āliyā*: while others have not attained the object [of their devotion], I alone am one who has attained it. Thinking, "She is my beloved," and because of the intensity of my love for her—she who dwells as my very life—when I call out the sacred name of the Great Lord (*Periyaperumāḷ*) and run about crying out, "O my beloved! O my beloved! she follows me, saying, "I too am devoted to him. Thus, having become utterly deluded by his words, I too have fallen into a state of madness.
Even if one were to kill me, there is no one who could carry me away or deceive me; for I am Māraṇār, the Infinite One, the Lord of the World,
the King, the Sovereign, and the Unfathomable.

Even though infinite supremacy exists within the human state, it is easy for one who acts with humility to attain it; however, those who remain arrogant and full of self-limitation do not. Nalanarāṇan, having embraced his own mother, Viṭamāṭṭāmai, caused her to shine with splendor.
Pitan, the destroyer of hell, through his own affection, would not allow even an enemy to stand in opposition to him as he dwelt together with her. For one who remains in this manner, there is Pitan.
Whether one is high or low,
there is no such thing as being born into this world without having sinned;
for even the noble Vāṇaṉ and Araṅkaṉ fell from their original state.
If one asks whether there is madness in the madman, there is indeed madness;

for the sake of worship, the body must be maintained, yet in that state where even the maintenance of the body is absent, all worldly affairs cease and there is only madness. There is no room for such madness within this circle [of existence]. Whether it be gold, base metal, water, grass, or even poison—all these are said to be "wealth" (vibhūti) by the ear, yet they are merely a means to ward off the enjoyments of *prakṛti*. Even in the midst of such "wealth," there is only madness.
The Lord of the Egg (Brahmā) is the sustainer of all that exists within the Egg.
Since he must remain as its sustainer, he resides in the temple, ever-present and easily accessible.

When his own son, Vāyu, who was born at the beginning of the Kalpa, became intoxicated and descended here saying, "I am he," the Lord himself provided him with the means to overcome his obstacles. He is my father.

If one were to treat that madman with medicine, would he not become even more intoxicated by the sweet flavors? Would he ever cease from his wicked deeds—his vices and his addiction to liquor—merely because of the qualities and efforts of those who care for him?
If he does not stop, will he not continue to act in such a way that he ruins himself and brings ruin upon others as well?
Is there no policy to restrain him? Indeed, there is none.
The noble one has come;
he who is the beloved of Tamarai, the Lord of Maṇavāḷam, has come to this place, having crossed over the sea of suffering.

He has come to bestow the fruit of the twenty-two [verses] upon those who know him, saying, "I shall grant you the means for the practice of spiritual discipline (sādhanānuṣṭhāna). Thus it is said. He shines forth, having crossed over the ocean of worldly existence, which is difficult to traverse, by means of his own power. To those who seek him, he provides the means for the performance of spiritual practice; indeed, he stands ready to grant them their desires. Thus, in the twenty-second [verse], it is proclaimed that he dwells within the heart of the seeker.
It is not as if one must practice this Nīti for its own sake; nor is it that one must practice the other puruṣārthas (aims of human life) merely for their own sake.
Rather, he who declares through the authoritative scriptures that there is an object to be worshipped (upāsya-vastu) descended as the incarnation known as Ayyāṉ Oṉṉāta-paṭi, who is easily accessible.

Having obtained the sacred water (tīrtha) as an incarnation of Araṅkaṉ, he dwelt in the temple, remaining ever present there. He was the beloved of the Great Warrior (Periya Pirāṭṭiyār), who was like a mother to him; he was her very own son, Maṇavāḷaṉ, born from her womb. I am his son, for those who were dear to him were indeed my own kin. When he went out to the forest, his mother would follow behind him; she remained a witness to the offenses he committed, which caused her heart to burn with grief, yet she stood by him as the very embodiment of human effort (puruṣakāra).

Do not speak thus; for that splendor is immeasurable. He who is the beloved of the Lord of the Fishermen, he who is the great majesty praised by Ākaiyār, he who dwells within the realm of the Pittan—I am he.
Thus, even if others should speak falsely, let them be struck down; I alone am the one who possesses the essence of the Karu.
Whether it be the gods or mortals, whether it be the wise or the ignorant, there is no one who can stand before me;
for every single step I take upon this earth, my feet tread upon those who have already perished.
Whether it be the impurity of today or the purity of tomorrow, or even the beauty of the future, there is no connection between them and me as I walk. There is no relationship whatsoever.

If one were to ask whether there is any lack of detachment from worldly existence or any lack of devotion toward service for that single person who has attained the Lord, even Brahmā and the other gods would consider their own prosperity as mere straw.
Since the Lord is the father of the immortals and the immortals are His servants,
and since all the eternal deities come to experience Him, why should all those in the world not go to the temple and attain Him with ease?
Thinking, "Even the six flavors are but transformations of bile," he went to the physician.
In that city, there was a man who had mastered the entire collection of the eight branches of medicine;
he took him as his own dear friend.
When I am thinking, "I am my own master," and when that bile (pitta) arises within me, what answer can I give to the Lord?
This is the meaning of the verse. "How could I have obtained this other shore?"—it is not as if I obtained it by my own power; they say that I obtained it by the power of the Lord of All.

Even in this world, for one who converses with those who are not devotees of the Lord, all desired human goals (puruṣārthas) will be unobtainable; my mother and I shall fall into calamity. Even if someone were to attain all human goals by deceiving others, there would be no merit in it; my mother and I would suffer the loss of our lives. Thus, having cast off his own mind which had become agitated, and having severed his own delusion as if cutting through a creeper, he remained, having made his heart firm toward the Supreme.
Thinking, "He who was my master has become my servant," I remained indifferent;
yet, as he entered the temple and cried out, "I am easily accessible to anyone who comes," I felt a surge of resentment.

As he approached me, I thought, "How can I show such hostility toward this man who has rendered me such great service by freeing me from my preoccupation with worldly objects? Thus, I became his servant.
"Whosoever among my own people, whoever else, and even this man here— each one of them shall be struck down by me;
I shall destroy them all," thus did I resolve in my mind.
"Who is this person who comes to me?
What is his descent?"—thus I asked my father. "Everyone is a relative; one is related to another through their kin, and I consider them all to be my own relatives," he replied.

"O father, let everyone abandon the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) that lead to worldly existence and cast off these unstable, material enjoyments (*prākṛtabhoga*); tell me, who are those who remain as 'father'? Thus I spoke.
Thinking, "Among all these people, there is not even one who can see with his own eyes," the king remained in a state of delusion. Then the sages said, "He is indeed here.

"Where is he? "Right here. "How could I speak of him as being elsewhere when he is right here? "He has indeed seen with his own eyes; having cast off his former body, he has descended [into this one] and made his own limbs my own."

"I have come here because I wish to see you face-to-face. Having heard the sacred name of Periya Perumāḷ, who graced the Kaṇvaḷar at the Koil on the banks of the Talaikkaṭṭātaṭi river—the very first among the incarnations—I have been filled with longing and have come.
Why do you not look upon me now? Why do others disregard me, saying, 'He is a beggar'?
Thus did he speak, and the Lord took his hand and led him inside.
He thought:
"Who among the great Pāṇḍyas will come to my aid? Who is the Kulacekaraṇ who dwells in Koṅkaṇa?
Even among the Colas, there is not one who can help these cowherds."
Even if my life were to end today, there is no other refuge for me than the feet of the Lord who dwells upon the mountain of Aruṅgaṉaṭi;

there is no other land to go to but the sacred feet of the Lord who dwells upon the mountain of Aḻakiyamaṇavāḷ. There is no one else besides these two who has ever been so intensely devoted to the Lord as I have been, nor is there anyone else who has loved Him with such total devotion. O Lord, you alone know the depth of my heart.
This was granted by Śrī Kulaśekhara Perumāḷ, who acted as the administrator for the maintenance of Koṅkar Koṉ Kulacekaraṉ during the Chola war.

For this cowherd, there is no such thing as "one"; for other cowherds, there is no such thing as "two. What is this "one"? It is the touch of one who is not a devotee (*abhāgavataspṛś*); it is the state of being devoid of inclination toward the Blessed One (*bhagavad-pravaṇya*). There is not a single day in this entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) where such suffering does not exist. This condition of suffering exists in every place. Even for those who have realized this, there is no place in this world where that condition does not exist.

The introduction: May there arise a desire for the knowledge of the Blessed One; may there arise a renunciation of other objects; may there arise the inclination and the capacity to experience those who possess superior qualities; may there arise the capacity to experience those who have attained the fullness of internal virtues; and may there arise the conviction that "the elders are seated upon our own shoulders"—and furthermore, may the elders also grant their consent within that assembly which has thus been formed. Thus far.

Whether it be the state of being the object of the Lord (*bhagavad-viṣayatvam*), or the state of being the object of a devotee (*bhāgavata-viṣayatvam*), or the state of being favorable (*ānukūlyam*), once one has acted with such sincerity as to abandon all other objects and focus solely on Him, and having thereafter removed all opposition, even those who have never before seen the attainment of the Lord can perceive it. Or, as for Rāvaṇa himself—whether he says "I am He" or "He shall stand upon my head"—there is no contradiction in his speech.

To this, he replied: "There is indeed another heart; listen. Having attained the Lord immediately upon the fall of the body, that Kṣatriya body remains in the midst of enjoyments until its end. Even after exhausting those enjoyments at the conclusion of the body, one attains the Lord through the sequence of the *piṇḍa* (the subtle body). Thus I have explained it to you. Having said this, he remained there for six days, and the king also stayed there, having received [the teaching] within his heart.

He who, having reached that mountain Veṅkaṭam—which he had sought out by following the path of his own destiny—remained there; and he who remained there while the ministers and the forest-dwellers were clearing the forest on Mount Veṅkaṭam; and he who, having experienced the inner realization of the Great Lord (Periyaperumāḷ), cast off all worldly attachments and remained at Tirumalai to perform service, dwelling upon the sacred feet of the Lord of Tiruveṅkaṭam with devotion, yet feeling a sense of aversion toward opposition.

They do not wait for the time when one must say, "I am bid farewell," but rather, "I am called hither. They do not wait for the time when one must say, "I am bidden adieu," but rather, "I am beckoned. They do not wait for the time when one must say, "I am bid goodby," but rather, "I am greeted. They do not wait for the time when one must say, "I am parted from," but rather, "I am met with. They do not wait for the time when one must say, "I am separated from," but rather, "I am united
Having entered the assembly hall of the three Vedas at Kūṉēru in my own Veṅkaṭam, I shall sing the *avatārikai* (introductory verses) of the *Mutal Pāṭṭu*, beginning with "ūṉēṟ" and so forth.

I shall say: "To one who possesses the fitness for discerning between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, human birth is required; to one who desires to protect others exceedingly, the status of a *kṣatriya* is required; and to one who desires to dwell entirely within service (*kaiṅkarya*), even the state of an animal is better. Thus I shall speak.

If one asks, "Why must I endure this suffering for this body?"—I reply: "Day by day, moment by moment, the body wastes away through the consumption of food rich in flesh, and the Self departs; thus, I must endure it. Furthermore, if one asks, "Why must I endure it even though the true nature of Dharma exists eternally?"—I reply: "It appears as if non-existent because of the contraction of knowledge (jñāna-saṅkoca);
it is because of this contraction of knowledge that I must endure it."

I am one who, having pierced the head of Yama with my spear, caused the gods to scatter sandalwood powder and sing his praises as they danced; I am that very person who dwells within the flute. I am he who possesses the wisdom of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*). I am he who, having realized the worthlessness of the body and the distinct nature of the Self, perceived that "I am the remainder" (*śeṣa*) within himself and that "he alone is the Lord.
Even though he was thus wandering through the sixty-four arts, he did not find any opposition there; rather, he found only those who were devoted to him in their service.

Another day, he sang of the Ṛṣabhas who were eager for union with their beloveds at the time of dawn. He sang: "I am the mother; my father, having conceived affection for me, follows his son; I have no other refuge but you, O Mother. And saying, "I am everything," and "O Mother, I am the earth," he sang of the refuge of the earth, and thus he performed the daily service with a heart delighting in servitude.

The Lord of the Discus (Viṣṇu) entered the hall and sat with palms joined in reverence and head bowed; he remained there, holding Śrīpāñcajanya, who was stationed at the gateway of the palace of the Lord of the Earth (Brahmā), who had entered the hall while experiencing the divine presence. Those present in the hall saw him there; those in the courtyard said that the Lord of the Sacred Footprints (Brahmā) was there, having come by the path of the gods; and those in the inner sanctum said it was the hand of the Lord of the Sacred Mark (Śiva), which had emerged from his own mouth as he was chewing betel leaf. Thus they spoke of them one after another.
Thinking, "I shall go to that land which lies beyond the boundary of Veṅkaṭa," he reached Tirumalai;

there, having crossed the Koṇeri river and entered the domain of the Kurukā Pirappan, he proceeded until he reached the Amānuva settlement, where he remained under the protection of the Kurukā Pirappan who dwells beyond the Tirukoṇeri.

Even if one were to live in a temple, one would only see it in Tirukoṇṇēri. While there are many words used to describe this body, the word "vāḷu" (temple) is used because it is indeed a dwelling for the Lord who exists in the form of *bhoga* (enjoyment).

The author says that although human birth is difficult to attain for the purpose of discerning between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and even more difficult to obtain for the sake of protecting others, one must nevertheless possess a *kṣatriya* birth, which is a meritorious body. This is due to the cause of his wickedness.

Having taught the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, Māṭṭāṭe instructed me on how to protect others. Even those born in sinful wombs, such as animals, and even those who have fallen from their caste—all these exist throughout the sacred Tirumalai. "What must I do? they asked. "I shall tell you," he replied. "I shall tell you what must be done for those who have fallen. "If one falls away from the path, will it not be seen? they asked. "Even those who have reached the highest state, even those who have attained the status of a *cūḍāla*, even those who possess wisdom, wealth, and jewels—I shall tell you what must be done for them."

The first verse: "Therefore, in the springtime at the sacred Tiruveṅkaṭa mountain, I shall go to the shore of the sea and dwell there. This is the introductory statement. Regarding the enjoyment of the fruits of one's actions (*bhoga*): whether they be finite or infinite, they exist within the realm of *saṃsāra*. Is it not said that such enjoyment exists even in heaven? If so, what is the water [of liberation] for which I long? They say that even the enjoyment on earth, attained through the grace of the Lord, is like a honeycomb dripping with sweetness. Even that enjoyment, when compared to the bliss of the Lord, is but a mere drop. Thus they speak.

What is the use of all this wealth? Let it be—whether one enjoys the celestial nymphs endowed with the splendor of youth as if they were a mere crest-ornament, or whether one dwells in the midst of those who possess the power to grant even the kingdom of heaven, or whether one possesses the sovereign glory of the earth—I have no need for these things to experience the pleasures of heaven and so forth. What do I say? I say: "I have no need for them"; that is to say, I have no need for the human ends (puruṣārtha) consisting of the enjoyment of those [pleasures]. Why do I say I have no need for them?
