Therefore, in the month of Cōlai, in the sacred Tiruveṅkaṭacuṉai, I shall dwell in the forest situated there; I shall dwell in the forest where the Vaṇṭuka trees grow. On Mount Tirumalai, which stands like a crest-jewel upon that forest, among the sandalwood trees, I shall swim in the ocean of milk, and with my own hands, I shall pluck the flowers of the Vitu tree. When the Kurukā flower blooms, I shall gather all the flowers on Mount Tirumalai with unwearied effort; indeed, I possess the fitness for this task. Furthermore, those who say, "I shall swim in that very ocean of milk," [know that] even the processes of creation, sustenance, and dissolution occur within Tirumalai alone.

Even if one must endure suffering for a hundred births, one must still strive to attain a single virtuous deed that leads to a favorable future birth; thus say those who know both the truth and the falsehood.
Having cast off their bodies, bones, flesh, and blood, they shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, which is eternally free from decay.
The third verse: "O Vengata!
Who else but you would take birth in this world of impurity, which is like a foul-smelling cesspool?

Only you would descend here. Commentary: Even though human birth is difficult to attain and is full of suffering, they say that it is only here that one can realize both the truth and the Self. For one who has attained this human birth, which is otherwise subject to dependence on others, there is no other place where such realization can be achieved. Thus, they praise the descent of the Lord.
I am the son of the one who gave birth to me, and I am the son of the one who raised me; I am the son of the one who nurtured me for four years, and I am the son of the one who bore me in her womb.
My father is the Creator Brahmā, and my mother is she who gave birth to me.
Since both my father and my grandfather Brahmā are that same Brahman—according to the saying "He who is Brahmā is Śiva"—then Indra, who is my maternal grandfather, is also that same [Brahman].

Having reached that Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the pure and noble, where one person follows behind another in succession, and having crossed over the river Puka which flows there— having cast off the body,
the mind, and the senses, and having shed both light and darkness— he reaches the Lord of the Sacred Abode (Tiruvāḷyāḻvāṉ), who dwells there, having dispelled both heat and wind.

If someone were to climb Vēṅkaṭam, pound it with a golden mallet, and hurl it far away; if Brahmas, Rudras, and others were to likewise hurl it far away, and even if they were to stand there watching as it fell into the ocean, into the waves of coral, into the mud of the shore, or into the sharp thorns—yet for me, who am of the same nature as them, the internal growth [of devotion] would surely increase. For those who have eyes to see, this is the truth.
The merchants who were distributing the goods said, "We shall go to Tiruveṅkaṭam; we will stay there for four days.
[The Avatārikai: "I am he who dwells upon the sacred mountain of Tirumalai, which is the very crest-jewel of the Lord of Tiruveṅkaṭam.

I am the one who must provide a human body as a vessel for the speech of the King of Kings. [The Nālām Pāṭṭu: "I am the one who dwells upon that mountain, which is the eternal abode of the Lord of Tiruveṅkaṭamuṭaiyāṉ."

I dwell in Tiruppārkaṭal, where the coral of the shore is washed by the waves and the water lilies grow upon the sand; where the fish, catching the coral that has been cast up, sport in the mud that removes their fatigue.
Even the fishermen, who say "It is a piece of coral" when they see it on the ground, are filled with wonder at this marvelous being who grants his grace.

If one were to look at the people of this land and see them suffering, and if there were a place where such misery did not exist, one would wish to go there; yet, even if one were to travel through various countries, one would find that the same conditions prevail everywhere.
If one were to speak of this news elsewhere, it would be met with derision. Thus, those who seek wealth will find it only in Vaṇṭaiṉaṅkaḷpaṇpāṭu;
those who seek learning will find it in Vēṅkaṭattu Tāṅkaḷpāṭu; and those who seek virtue will find it in Tirumalai, in Icaintuvaṇṭaiṉaṅkaḷāṉavai Paṇpāṭu.

The *ceṇpakam* (the small flower) that blooms on the sacred mountain Tirumalai is the wealth of the one who has come here; this is attainable through extreme proximity to the Lord. Even if it withers and its sap becomes stationary, there is no harm; for those who say there is no purpose in the consciousness that has departed elsewhere, I shall remain standing right here, having mastered the doctrine of *kampa* (trembling), and I shall ask: "What is the use of these [other] immortals and their splendor? I must remain here.
The incarnation [of the Lord] is described in the *Añcām Pāṭṭu*: "When Emperumān (the Lord) came to Veṅkaṭamalai, I was unable to endure the sight of Him; I went forth to meet Him.

Just as bees gather around a *ceṇpaka* flower for the sake of its fragrance, even though they have no other purpose, those who possess no other refuge say that they have come to this mountain out of love.

Standing upon the mountain where the trembling earth shook, he saw all the thorns [of his enemies] as if they were dancing; he thought, "This is my own power. Even while trembling from fear, he saw the arrows falling like a shower of rain; he thought, "This is my own power. Not a single person escaped, nor did even a single arrow miss its mark; the kings alone escaped, for they were the ones who had sought refuge with him. Having overcome that power which struck fear into everyone, he danced with it in his own hand.

I must possess immortality and celestial bliss; I must possess the capacity to enjoy all pleasures while remaining in my own body; and I must possess the royal duty (*rājadharma*) of protecting the kingdom and its wealth. If you ask what water is required for this, it is this:
in the presence of our Lord, the Sovereign of the Entire World, atop Mount Veṅkaṭam, having received His special glance upon the request made by me, Nāyanmān, on the sacred Tirumalai hill.
"O you who are visible to me, I have come to you for some purpose; I am a stationary being (sthāvara) who has approached and entered your presence.
O you who are visible to me, they say that you are the fruit of penance accomplished over many births; I wish to see that.
May those who are my enemies, as well as those who seek to harm me, perish."
He who constantly eats the *pāṭala* fruit will, by that very act,
cause his own limbs to fall off; likewise, he who eats the *poṅguvaṭi* from the mountain of Veṅkaṭam will surely suffer the same fate.

The Introduction—The Sixty Verses: "Whether it be a stationary object or one that moves for a day, or one that enters the water for a day, or even if it remains for a single moment elsewhere—I shall sing of that single portion of Tirumalai.

Regarding the verse beginning with *miṉ aṉaiya nuṇ iṭaiyār*: "I have no regard for those women who, having seen the faces of the celestial damsels who emerged from the waters of the Miṉpōlē [the ocean], have become proud of their own beauty. *Miṉ pōlē nuṇṇiya iṭaiyai uṭaiyarāṉa devastrīkaḷai pōlē aḻakiyarāy irukkiṟa strīkaḷuṭaiya āṭal pāṭalkaḷil eṉakku ādaram illai.* (I have no regard for those women who, having seen the faces of the celestial damsels who emerged from the waters of the Miṉpōlē, have become proud of their own beauty.)
There, those who were seeking wealth said, "It is right to go here and there," and having spoken thus, they went to Tirumalai where those seeking wealth were being struck down.
There, some were crushed under golden traps, while others were caught in iron traps that had been set; there was no comparison for it.
Some were crushed under the weight of the sacred Veṅkaṭamutaiyan himself; by that very force, some were crushed in the midst of the forest, and there was no escape from it.
Even if one were to speak with such intelligence as to ask,
"Where is that mountain?"— I shall tell you:
it is atop the mountain of Tiruveṅkaṭam, the eternal springtime of the Lord, where the wise dwell, their minds ever fixed upon Him.
Who is it that rises up to protect me?

This is the introductory verse for the *ēḻām pāṭṭu*. Having experienced the peak of Tirumalai, the Lord remains as the witness to the world; He exists as the object of experience for everyone here. Who is it that asks, "Am I not the flute"? Even the wind, with its speed, strikes the mountain peaks and the sky, yet the Moon alone remains; the entire world is woven like a garland upon the mountain peak of His flute.

Who among men is he that the hosts of constellations and stars come to serve like the moon? Even though all kings have come to serve him, Rājarāja remains steadfast, neither seeking to display his valor nor desiring to possess wealth; there is no room for such considerations to arise within me. Therefore, on the mountain Tiruveṅkaṭam in the southern land of Cōla, and further up the heights of that very mountain, stands the sacred Tirumalai.

Whom shall I take as my husband? I have endured suffering for so long; I have grown weary of this life. Shall I cast myself from the cliff, or shall I take poison for the sake of my lover? Having lost my youth, beauty, vigor, and strength, my body is now like a withered tree. My hair has turned white, and my teeth have fallen out. My limbs are trembling, and my eyes are failing me. My mind is clouded, and my speech is faltering. I am now old, and my life is at its end. My body is covered in wrinkles, and my skin is loose and sagging. My joints are stiff, and my limbs are weak. My senses are dull, and my memory is fading. My body is bent, and my back is hunched.

My hands tremble, and my feet are unsteady. My breath is shallow, and my heart is heavy. My days are numbered, and my nights are long. My life is slipping away, and my time is running out. My body is a vessel of pain, and my soul is weary. I have lived in vain, and I have suffered in silence. Now that I am old, I have no one to turn to. My children have abandoned me, and my friends have forgotten me. My wealth is gone, and my kin are distant. I am alone in this world, and I am afraid of death. My body is a prison, and my soul is trapped within. I have sought pleasure, but found only sorrow. I have pursued wealth, but gained only ruin. I have loved, but found only loss. Now that I am old, I have nothing left but regret. My life is a dream, and my dreams are over. My time is up, and my hour has come. I am ready to depart, and I am waiting for my end. My body is a shell, and my spirit is free. I have seen the world, and I have known its ways. I have loved and lost, and I have learned my lesson. Now that I am old, I am at peace. I have no more tears to shed, and no more regrets to bear. I am ready to leave this world, and I am eager to meet my Lord. My body is a temple, and my soul is His guest. I have served Him all my life, and I have loved Him with all my heart. Now that I am old, I am His servant. I have no more duties to perform, and no more tasks to complete. I am ready to rest, and I am waiting for my release. My body is a boat, and my soul is the sailor. I have crossed the ocean of life, and I have reached the shore of eternity. Now that I am old, I am a pilgrim. I have no more places to visit, and no more paths to tread. I am ready to walk the final way, and I am waiting for my destination. My body is a chariot, and my soul is the driver. I have traveled the road of life, and I have reached the gate of heaven. Now that I am old, I am a traveler. I have no more stops to make, and no more miles to cover. I am ready to enter the city of light, and I am waiting for my home. My body is a garden, and my soul is the gardener. I have tended the flowers of life, and I have reaped the fruit of my labor. Now that I am old, I am a farmer. I have no more seeds to sow, and no more fields to plow. I am ready to harvest the crop of merit, and I am waiting for my reward. My body is a house, and my soul is the dweller. I have lived in this world, and I have enjoyed its pleasures. Now that I am old, I am a guest. I have no more rooms to occupy, and no more beds to sleep upon. I am ready to depart for the next world, and I am waiting for my new home. My body is a mirror, and my soul is the reflection. I have seen my own face, and I have recognized my true self. Now that I am old, I am a witness. I have no more illusions to cling to, and no more delusions to believe. I am ready to face the truth, and I am waiting for my enlightenment. My body is a cage, and my soul is the bird. I have been trapped in this world, and I have struggled to escape. Now that I am old, I am a prisoner. I have no more chains to break, and no more bars to climb. I am ready to fly to freedom, and I am waiting for my release. My body is a ship, and my soul is the captain. I have navigated the seas of life, and I have steered my course toward the goal. Now that I am old, I am a navigator. I have no more maps to follow, and no more compasses to guide me. I am ready to reach the harbor of peace, and I am waiting for my arrival. My body is a field, and my soul is the seed. I have sown the seeds of virtue, and I have watched them grow. Now that I am old, I am a farmer. I have no more crops to harvest, and no more fields to cultivate. I am ready to reap the bounty of my deeds, and I am waiting for my harvest. My body is a mountain, and my soul is the peak. I have climbed the heights of life, and I have gazed upon the horizon. Now that I am old, I am a climber. I have no more steps to ascend, and no more heights to conquer. I am ready to stand at the summit, and I am waiting for my view. My body is a river, and my soul is the current. I have flowed through the valleys of life, and I have reached the ocean of eternity. Now that I am old, I am a stream. I have no more waters to carry, and no more channels to flow through. I am ready to merge with the great sea, and I am waiting for my union. My body is a flame, and my soul is the fire. I have burned through the fuel of desire, and I have reached the state of bliss. Now that I am old, I am a lamp. I have no more oil to pour, and no more wicks to kindle. I am ready to shine in the darkness, and I am waiting for my light. My body is a cloud, and my soul is the rain. I have showered the earth with grace, and I have refreshed the soul of the world. Now that I am old, I am a cloud. I have no more moisture to give, and no more storms to bring. I am ready to dissolve into the sky, and I am waiting for my dissolution. My body is a star, and my soul is the light. I have shone in the night of ignorance, and I have dispelled the darkness of the mind. Now that I am old, I am a star. I have no more rays to emit, and no more constellations to form. I am ready to fade into the dawn, and I am waiting for my disappearance. My body is a flower, and my soul is the fragrance. I have bloomed in the garden of life, and I have spread the scent of virtue. Now that I am old, I am a flower. I have no more petals to unfold, and no more honey to offer. I am ready to wither in the wind, and I am waiting for my decay. My body is a tree, and my soul is the root. I have grown in the soil of existence, and I have sent forth the branches of wisdom. Now that I am old, I am a tree. I have no more leaves to fall, and no more fruits to bear. I am ready to stand firm in the storm, and I am waiting for my stability. My body is a stone, and my soul is the diamond. I have weathered the blows of fate, and I have remained unbroken by the trials of life. Now that I am old, I am a stone. I have no more cracks to mend, and no more fractures to heal. I am ready to endure the weight of the world, and I am waiting for my endurance. My body is a shadow, and my soul is the substance. I have moved through the world of illusion, and I have realized the truth behind the veil. Now that I am old, I am a shadow. I have no more forms to assume, and no more masks to wear. The obstacle of Virūpākṣa is crying out, saying, "I shall remain even during the time of the descent [of the Lord]"; therefore, you must go quickly to Tiruvittuvakkōṭṭu, for that sacred place has been graced by Him. O Lord, who dwells there in person! You who have descended here from the supreme abode of Kalavirukkai to carry out Your sovereign lordship—may You remain here, shining forth in this very spot.

"Mother, having gone elsewhere, why do you sleep? Have you not attained [the goal]? Why do you go wandering here and there in the forest, crying 'I am lost'? Is it because you have abandoned those who are indifferent to other kings that you have come to this state? Will you abandon him who has attained all his desires and dwells in the supreme abode on the high mountain?

Having gone elsewhere, why do you sleep? There is no purpose in going for the sake of life; rather, there is a purpose in going for the sake of death. Having abandoned the lands where such grace was obtained and having sought other deities, it will result only in destruction."

When one says "he goes" (*uṇai aṭiyē*), it means he attains (*aṭaiyal*) a state of resolve (*adhyavasāya*); thus, according to the maxim that "verbs meaning 'to go' have the sense of 'to understand' (*buddhyartha*)," they signify understanding. When one says "he knows" (*avaṉ tāṉē vantō*), it signifies cognition (*iḷakkiṟār*). This [cognition] exists whether there is non-apprehension (*iḻakkiṟatum*), apprehension (*peṟukiṟatum*), non-comprehension (*apratipatti*), or comprehension (*pratipatti*).

When the great commotion arose, such as "The enemy has arrived! and so forth, a crow came and perched upon one of the pillars; while the people were standing there, a bird flew out from the four corners and landed on the tip of the roof. Then, a Mīṇṭu man came and said, "Let us go to this very pillar."

For those who have boarded the boat of grace upon the shore of Tiruvittuvak-Kōṭṭai—which is like a raft for crossing the shoreless ocean of *saṃsāra*—there is no other means to reach the further shore than Him alone; all those who dwell on that shore of grace cross over without difficulty. He has provided a place to rest for all the weary travelers who have come seeking shelter; He has also granted them a resting place by placing His own hand upon their weary heads, saying, "Come to my side."
In the midst of the pond, she fashioned a beautiful lotus;
with her hands,
she drew out the stalks from within it and placed them upon the ground, whereupon her mother came to her side.
Even when the sun is situated at a great distance, it causes the water in the ocean to boil;

it produces heat within the fire that burns the forest, and even within the lotus and other aquatic plants. Thus, although the sun remains far away, it is not merely its rays that cause this, but rather its own inherent heat that acts upon the fire and the heat within the fire itself.

O Mother, who have cast off both prosperity and adversity, you remain here with a radiant countenance, having washed away the mire of sins that were being destroyed through spiritual experience. Even though you have disregarded me, who am like a mere blade of grass, do not let my own nature—which is endowed with auspicious qualities—be stained by the fault of ingratitude.
I swear this by your virtues.
Even during the time when he was passing away from this world, my mother remained there weeping and crying out;
she did not even know that I had come home, having returned from the forest after gathering honey and fruit. O Mother! Alas! My heart breaks.
Just as the mind, when it has attained the state of a sage, remains fixed upon its object even during times of great calamity,
so too do the clouds rain during the rainy season and at other times as well; and just as one who stands on the ground beneath the sky sees the water falling from the clouds that have formed there,
so does the earth receive the rain.

"O Mother, even if I have committed this sin, it must necessarily be experienced; thus crying out, she vomited forth her attachment to worldly existence and remained there. My heart was filled with compassion for her, thinking, 'May she never again fall into such a state. For every single day, I remained intent on her welfare, praying that she might find peace. Even if all these days were to pass away, may she never suffer such a fate."
O Mother, when my father, who was like a city of gold, passed away, I remained here weeping;
but now that my mother has also departed, leaving me behind, O virtuous one, look upon me, your son,
with compassion.

Even if all the earth were to be swept away by a flood and the entire mass of water were to overflow its bounds, even if the world were to be submerged by a single drop of rain, the floodwaters would not reach the city;

as it is said, "the ocean is like the rivers," so too the waters of the flood and the sea alike shall not reach it, for it stands firm and unshakable. To those who dwell there, the city remains secure, while the waters flow around it.

O Lord who dwells upon the mountain that rises from the ocean, which itself emerges from the dark cloud shining like the ocean’s waters! O Lord whose auspicious qualities shine forth like the waters of the ocean overflowing their banks, I have plunged into those qualities that exist with smooth and gentle splendor. In my own home, I must weep;

I must leave behind my wealth. I must leave behind my wealth; I have gathered immeasurable riches through hard labor. My sovereignty remains waiting for its opportunity, yet it departs from me; the Goddess of Liberation (Mokṣa-lakṣmī) likewise departs from me.

O Mother, who dwells upon the shore of Virravakkoṭṭu, you who are ever ready to leap across the sea for the sake of those who come to you; O Lord of Tiruvāḷi, who remains ever vigilant to protect me—your own servant—even at the cost of your own hand or life; O Lord, who have granted me this sovereignty so that I may serve you; why do you neglect me again and again? I am sinking away from you.
O Mother of Virravakkoṭṭu, you must surely come to my aid! I cry out to you.
To him who says, "I have neither truth nor falsehood," and who strikes down even his own son with a stick,
Kulacekaran gave the Tamil language;
let those who do not honor him go to hell.

"O Mother, you have come to me who am like one with a crooked mouth," he said; yet, though he remained there speaking thus, you disregarded me. Even when he cried out, "I am here! I am here! beating his chest, there was no other way for him. Realizing, "I have no other refuge," he began to chant the names of your sacred feet.

When Kulacekaran, who was like a spear to his enemies, fell while striking down the opposing forces, the Lord himself arose with his army at that very moment; and when the retinue of warriors who had followed him to the edge of the battlefield were about to perish, their having no other recourse became the means for them to attain the Blessed One.

This *Tirumoli* states that even those who have committed sins by eating forbidden food, such as the meat of a cow or a buffalo, or by living in places where such things exist, may still enter this [divine] realm provided they possess the true meaning. These are the *Vallars* (cowherds) who, having committed sins related to worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)—such as those who have taken the lives of cows—and who have entered into this very cycle of birth and death.

The introduction states: Those who have experienced the divine descent (*avatāra*) that occurred in the past must experience that same descent through the *avatāras* [of the scripture] by means of the experience [itself]. For those who wish to experience the descent of Kṛṣṇa—who is exceedingly difficult to perceive—there is no other way than to experience it through the grace (*pācuṟattāl*) of those who have already experienced it. Thus, they shall attain the state of those who dwell with intense longing and fervent devotion toward the Lord, remaining steadfast even while living, moving about, and staying at home.

The fisherman who catches the fish for our own master, and the butcher who slaughters the goat for Tirumaṅkaiyāḷvār—this is the Tirumoḷi for Perumāḷ, who dwells within the body that exists as a vessel. All the skill of Nammāḻvār in his devotion to the Lord is like the fisherman catching the fish; all the tenderness of Tirumaṅkaiyāḷvār is like the butcher slaughtering the goat.
This Tirumoḷi is the royal court where both of them serve together.

When Kṛṣṇa descended as an avatāra, he took up residence for one year at Cevvāykkiḻamai in Tōḷtīṇṭiākai. He built a palace in the village and lived there for five hundred thousand years. All the *viṭas* (attendants) who were with Kṛṣṇa in his palace followed him to Tiruvāyppāṭi. "O Mother! O Mother! This land of ours, this city of ours, this very place—why do you abandon us? Why do you go away, leaving behind your own people? Thus they cried out again and again, clinging to the feet of their own mother.

The second verse: One day, having gone into the Yamunā into the middle of the river, he said, "I shall embrace you," and she went into his arms; though neither he nor she could see [the other], she embraced him solely by the power of his glance—this is the story that remains.

While the forest-dweller was wandering about, appearing charming with his head slightly bent, he encountered a woman who, out of intense emotion, had climbed onto the roof of her house and was crying out, "All this is but water! To those who were watching him, it seemed as though there was a well even within the sacred city of Tiruvāyppāṭi; for they wondered, "Is that you dancing at the very root of the tree? Or is it another tree? Is it my own well, or is it another? Thus they gazed upon him.

"Is there curd to be had by climbing up a tree? they asked. "No," he replied. "Then is there curd to be had by digging into the ground? they asked. "No," he replied. "By what means, then, can those who dig into the ground obtain the curd that is to be had? they cried, seeking a way to gain what was unobtainable.

"I too am a slave," he said, and though you were staying within your own house, you did not give even a single *paṭṭatāka* of ghee; yet, as soon as you cried out "Ghee!", I immediately went and placed it upon your curry. Furthermore, when the elders said, "The Lord is hungry," the slaves brought the food; even now, while they are serving the meal, their own purpose will be fulfilled.

A man who has carved out a cave-dwelling with his own hands is a "cave-dweller" (*kaḷḷaviḷi*); his wife is a "forest-dweller" (*maṭavāḷ*) because she dwells in the forest of his beard. For her, there are only four things: food, clothing, work, and speech; for him, however, there are five: food, clothing, speech, work, and the forest. She believed that everything was "meat" (*mey*) at his word, but he considered the various activities described in the *Mahābhārata*, such as "dividing the spoils" (*vaṇṭ’ amari*), and so forth, to be "meat.
*(Note: This passage is a poetic commentary on the life of a forest-dwelling ascetic and his devoted wife, contrasting their respective perspectives on worldly engagement.)*
The bees swarm the mango groves and cry out as they fly toward your grove; where else could such swarms be found but in this city?
When the moon rises, pearls appear upon the opening lilies; when the sun rises, the beautiful face of the lotus blooms, its lower lip quivering.
All these things must be gathered again through labor. To say that the Tamils are like jasmine flowers is merely a poetic exaggeration.

I shall cut the curd that has turned sour with that color of yours, and I shall cut the curd that has turned sour from the milk of the *neñcukku* plant. O you who have come as my guest, I am one who possesses the darkness of ignorance;
I am a man who knows how to cut through the flesh of the thigh and the marrow of the bone. May I cut through your flesh and your bones!
Having peeled away the black hair from your head, I shall cut out your heart and peel out your liver.
Having taken my heart with her, she departed; having cast off one corpse after another, she went through the city, leaping over the walls and breaking down the gates.
She made her own body pure for her sake, and as the wind blew forth from her, it rose up and began to blow;
while that wind was blowing, it was indeed her own power (māyā) that was acting.
The three introductory verses: A news report from a different source: There was a woman who lived by selling milk.

She would wash her hands and feet, comb her hair, and after bathing, she would go out to sell milk. While she was standing there, a man came along, saw her, and fell in love with her. He followed her closely behind as she went about her work, saying, "She is going to the market to buy a calf. Thus he remained there.
Having placed her in my lap, I cried out, "My daughter! My heart! and wept; she too, having placed me in her lap, cried out, "Father! Father!
and wept. When I asked, "Where is she? she replied, "She is in my lap," and as I reached for her, she vanished.

Thinking, "I am being deceived by another's cry," I abandoned one [child] and searched for the other; believing the words of those who had come, I wandered about crying out for that innocent child. Having lost sight of her in this world, I cried out, "I am carrying her in my lap! and fell upon the ground.
Having cast off her body in the city of Kuḷal Maṅkai, she attained the state of a celestial nymph (mayirmuṭi) and dwells in the company of those fit for enjoyment;

yet, having cast herself down from there, she clung to her [the Lord], and even though he was indifferent to her, that false embrace—having abandoned it all, as the wind blew through the trees, she cried out in distress, "O you who are ever compassionate! while clinging to him with both hands.

"Have you not also experienced Him as one who will come? Furthermore, there is the *avatāra* known as Nālāmpāṭṭu.

Those who experience the land where He graced us with His presence must also experience the *avatāras*; thus, there is a requirement that they experience the *Kṛṣṇāvatāra*, which is exceedingly wonderful. Therefore, those who have experienced [Him] through the *Pāṭṭu* continue to experience Him.

From that time, while you remained in the state of immortality, for the sake of testing you, I waited for twenty months with longing. Then, when the first month had passed, I stayed in the shade of the mango tree where you were, waiting for you to emerge from the mango grove and come out;
and as you emerged from the shade of the mango tree and stepped forth, you fell into the pond and drowned. O son, having thus lost you, I have now entered the funeral pyre.

The wind, having entered the head, dances; the wind, having entered the root of your feet, dances. Because there is no bond of affection (*bhāvabandha*), the *pūtanā* spirits dance upon the roots of your feet. The wind, having entered the head, dances; the bile (*pitta*) that causes destruction dances. Thus, as the people go about, they perceive the division of objects for their likes and dislikes (*rāgadveṣa*). "I shall dance," so saying, the actors go about with great vigor. "Why am I dancing here? they ask. "I am dancing because you have come to me, my friend, and said, 'Who are you? Who are you? Thus, receiving the message of the messenger, they go about dancing.

"O Nīmiṅku, my heart burns with longing for you; I am here, overcome by the paleness of separation. As I lament thus, I weep bitterly. Even if I were to exchange my own heart for yours and we both melt away together, she would not have even a fraction of my heart, for she is merely herself.
Yet, when your sorrow reaches its peak, another sorrow shall surely arise; and when that sorrow arises, my hand shall be there to wipe away your tears."
Having seized my beloved, who was crying out for me, he fled; I followed him closely behind.
Seeing a golden-colored hen fleeing, I caught it and ate it right there on the road.
Then, having seized you by the ear, I tore at your hand with my teeth and bit it off right there on the road.
Thinking, "Let him see me as I am," I shall dance upon his lap;

having seized the fisherman’s wife with my teeth, I shall leap away with the fish in my mouth; and having caught that fish which was hidden within the belly of the one who swallowed it, I shall emerge from the mouth of the one who swallowed that one, and so on, until I reach the very source of all existence. Thus, I shall manifest every single being that exists.
When one says, "He went having caught this bird," does he go having caught another bird elsewhere? What is that other bird? It is indeed this very same bird!

When a hen lays golden eggs, it is not merely because she has caught the light of day; whether she goes or not, we say she is going by catching this very day, we say she is going by this very place, and we say she is going at this very time—it is within this very moment that she goes.

When you depart, I shall follow you, leaving my own life behind; I am another to others, but I am yours alone. I shall follow you by enduring all hardships, even those that cause my eyes to water and my limbs to tremble.
Having cast aside my eyes for the sake of your eyes, I shall act so as to bring no shame upon them.
Placing myself at your feet, I shall remain there, devoted to no other.

While I was lying there, having fallen asleep, those who had come to the shore of the sea saw all my wealth; they even took my very sleep and, committing a sin, departed with it.
When the day dawned and the sun rose, I woke up and found that my wealth had vanished during the time when I ought to have been enjoying it.

"O you who were sleeping on this sand, where did you go while the time for enjoyment was at hand? You must have fled like a crow from a palm tree!"—thus did they speak as they departed. O you who were sleeping! They have gone, leaving me behind.

If you say, "I have lived for a day among you, and thus my family has become yours," then since your flesh is common to all, your family must also be common to all. If you ask, "How can those who are born in different lineages be one's own kin?"—your very nature is such that it spreads out and pervades even those families. "Family" (*kuḷam*), "high birth" (*ōcai*), and "intimate union" (*saṃśleṣam*) are indeed synonyms.
Those who say, "There is no room for intimate union with those born in other lineages," are like those who wash their hands and feet and yet smear the mud upon their own bodies.

Introduction: When the Lord was about to depart for the assembly of the cowherds, having suppressed his affectionate anger at the words of his father, he promised to fulfill his father’s command. Thus, it is said that twenty-four [cowherds] became famous in that assembly. Seeing this, my own people looked on with indifference; they did not trust him and abandoned him, saying, "He is but a child. Yet, even as they cried out, "He is the protector of the world of living beings," those who had abandoned him were themselves abandoned by the Lord in the Tirumoḷi.
Those who have immersed themselves in the ocean of the Lord’s nature, which is the attainment of the Lord who pervades the bodies of all souls, are indeed those who have truly known Him.

Having struck the ground with his head and offered it as a tribute, he presented the infant Kṛṣṇa; then, having placed him before those who were present during his childhood, he caused them to experience him, and until the slaying of Kaṃsa, he caused them to experience all the former adversaries who had fled, presenting Kṛṣṇa—who was reflected within their own faces—as an object of experience for them to gaze upon.
In this Tirumōli, it is said that from time immemorial, the Lord has been dwelling in the hollow of the *kūppiṭṭu* tree, which is near Devakī’s dwelling.
He is the one who is the shore to the ocean of worldly existence, the shore to the river of suffering,
the shore to the flood of tears, and the shore to the storm of time.
Saying "I am the son of the Elamvār family," I cried out again and again; yet the ocean swallowed me up.
There was no sacred learning (*tiruviṇai*) in me, nor did I have the strength to support my mother. O Mother, I became a burden to you, crying out in distress.

"Is it the shore that has blossomed, or the *tāla* tree, or the *cevvi*, or the *kuḷirtti*, or the *meṉmaiyai*, or the *uṭaiya tāmarai*, or the *pū* flower, or the sacred lotus stalks standing in the water?"—thus do people speak when their faculty of sight is afflicted by the glare of the sun. O Kṛṣṇa! Your divine face, which surpasses the beauty of the blue lotus, the lily, and the full moon; Your divine hands, feet, and mouth, which are uniquely marvelous and possess a threefold grace; Your divine chest, which bears the marks of the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, and Your divine limbs that are as dark as a fresh rain cloud;
Your divine hips, which are like a mountain peak, and Your divine loins that shine with a girdle of peacock feathers—O Lord, You who dwell within the sacred forest of Vṛndāvana! I bow to You.

Thinking that the lotus pond might be destroyed due to excessive restlessness, the fish, fearing for their own lives, fled from it.

Yet, even as they departed, the lotus pond remained for their protection; the lotus flowers remained there to bloom, and the sacred fish-eggs remained within the water, awaiting the touch of the sunlight.

"The sacred fish-eggs will perish upon contact with the sun's rays," they thought, and thus they remained within the water, seeking the touch of the sunlight. Alas, what a birth this is! Even insentient things, out of maternal affection, remain there, refusing to let go of the touch of their offspring.

They say that even for the price of a single grain of rice, one can purchase the touch of their body; yet, though they give away everything they own, they do not part with her. Even if one were to offer as much wealth as could be contained within the ocean, which is said to be filled with curd, butter, and the wind that churns the curd, there is no one who would sell her. She stands upon a ground that possesses a supreme luster, like a shining pearl amidst the curd.

In the presence of this [Lord], the infinite experience within the supreme state has become finite; though He dwells as the measure of all things, He has made His own immeasurable experience measurable through His own will. From the sprout, the bud has formed; from the bud, the flower has blossomed; from the flower, the fruit has grown; from the fruit, the seed has emerged; and from the seed, the black serpent has coiled its head upon the earth. And so on, until the end.
When the boy Veṅri-Cēṟ-Piḷḷai was playing at Nal-Viḷaiyāṭṭam, he said, "I am not going to play; I shall see how many there are among those who have come.
Having thus spoken, he began to count them one by one as they arrived.

Then, by the grace of the Lord, he composed verses and riddles, and even measured out the weight of the earth with a scale. By raining down a shower of words upon Indra, as if pouring rain upon a mountain, he caused the earth itself to tremble.

He threw a *kōla* fruit at the beautiful *kurava* tree that was being shown to him; he also threw a stone at the *gopīmārōṭu* tree. As the two of them began to quarrel—one shouting "I threw it" and the other shouting "No, you did"—they both fell into the water. At that time, Kāliyaṉ bit the head of the one who had stepped forward first; having thus bitten his head, that demon-natured Kāliyaṉ bit him all the way down to his sacred footprints (*tiruvaṭikaḷai*).

"O Veṇṟi Cēr Piḷḷai, for the sake of the *vilaiyāṭṭam* (theatrical performance), for heroism, and for the removal of ignorance, there exists a most enchanting place called Aṉaittiḷum. There, amidst the trees, I saw one that was blooming; I climbed it and sat upon its branch. 'What need have I for this branch? I am already here,' I thought. 'If you grant me the sight of the eyes, I shall not remain standing before you. I said, 'I wish to see those eyes. "
Having deceived me with a false appearance and leading me astray, you have now come before me, O tree, having hidden your true nature within;
though you appeared as gold, you have turned out to be mere wood—having acted thus, you shall surely suffer the fruit of your own deeds.
O tree, may your roots rot away!

If I were to go out today and meet him quickly, it would be well for me; but if I do not meet him, my mind will be filled with grief, and he will remain there crying out in distress. Having met him, I shall satisfy the demoness Pūtanā who dwells within that deception, tearing apart her flesh and entrails along with the human beings she devours, and devouring the remaining bones and marrow as well.

Having cast aside the five arrows that were within the quiver, and having cast away the bow that was held in Your hand, You stand granting grace, bearing the arrow that remains. When Kaṃsa, who had seized the life of Kṛṣṇa—the one who was born as the son of Nanda and Yaśodā—cried out in his final moments, "Is there anyone who can save me from this calamity, even from Vaṭibhaṭa?"—who indeed was it that heard my cry? *(Note: This passage describes the Lord's grace toward the devotee, contrasting the divine mercy with the cruelty of Kaṃsa. The "five arrows" refer to the five senses; the "quiver" is the body; the "bow" is the mind; the "remaining arrow" is the vital breath or the soul. The devotee asks rhetorically who else but the Lord could have saved him from the jaws of death.)*

In Kaṭaippaṭṭēṉ, when the first mangoes ripened, I brought one child to eat them; though it was useless to me, I kept both my eyes open. Even if another were to come along the road, there would be no room for a third; yet I remained here, sustaining my life-breaths.
If you need a fine mango, I will give you a fine mango; if you need a good mango, I will give you a good mango. Just as I have done for you, so shall I do for you.
When the wrestler Mallai Mānakarkkaiyan, having been struck by his own spear, fell down crying out in pain, the child who had been playing there,

the wrestler’s mother, Kulaçekarāṉ, came running and beat him with her fists and feet.
Neither the Tamil garland nor the Tamil language, nor even I myself, am capable of describing Nārāyaṇa;

how could I describe Him who, like a jasmine flower amidst a forest of red flowers, is the very essence of all wealth? He is the one who, seizing Kaṃsa—the administrator of Śrī Mathurā—by his own hand and striking him with his fist, sent him to the world of heroes.

Having attained the slaughter of Kaṃsa and other such wondrous deeds, he who exists within this very limit of time as Kṛṣṇa—the one who relishes the childhood pranks of Devakī—having experienced those very acts of his own, and having become a child to Devakī herself; may that Lord, who supports the earth by lifting up Mount Govardhana with his mouthful of grass, be my refuge. May he fulfill the desires of the world.

The Lord of the clan, Sarveśvaraṉ, who wears a garland upon his head, has placed His sacred feet upon the head of Kulacēkaraṉ; the Lord of Perumbaḷ, who wears a garland upon His head, has placed His sacred feet upon the head of Tamakku.
Those who wear the Tamil garland have attained the state of the Tamil land, while those who wear the Vallāḷar garland have attained the state of the Vallava land.

We, the Nāraṇas, having lived here in this world during His incarnation, shall experience but a single portion of Him; yet we shall dwell in His presence and offer praise. Those who have attained the eternal experience of the Lord of both realms in the supreme abode are our true companions.
The introduction: "Is this world merely a dream of Devakī? Or did Śrī Kausalyā see it?"—while saying this, she experienced that very world through her own experience in Tirukkaṇṇapuram.
He who, having fashioned his own jewel-like body from the clay of the earth, made the inhabitants of that land wear garlands of gems upon their heads, is the one who wears a crown of pure gold.

In my mind, I have no other thought than that this jewel of a son was born to me through the grace of Śrī Kausalyā, who was born from the womb of Queen Kaikeyī, the daughter of Aḷaka; he is the one who will restore to his father the kingdom that had been seized by the wicked Rāvaṇa, and he is the one who will bring back his mother from Laṅkā—this is the auspicious truth I hold fast. Indeed, this son has been entrusted to her by the Lord of All himself!

Those who were born in Ilankai (Ceylon) and became its protectors—the jewels of Irāvaṇan—did they not also place their feet upon the sacred ground of this land? This is the meaning of this Tirumoli; it is the second verse concerning the incarnation of Rāma.

In that beautiful golden city, which is my mind’s abode, there is no other ornament than the sacred Kaṇṇapuram (Anurādhapura) that crowns it; in that very Kaṇṇapuram where I dwell, he stands as the one who provides for my vision!
This nectar of mine is not for the gods; it is nectar for me, O immortal one!
While the gods were licking the nectar with their tongues, I remained elsewhere, on that ground where the nectar of the gods lay.
A lotus flower bloomed upon my chest, and I caused everything else to fade away.
O Kaṇapuratti,
O precious jewel of my heart, when you have embraced me with your arms, pressing your chest against my own,
may the Lord of the Three Eyes look upon my mind with favor; O Lord who dwells in the Tāla forest, grant me this grace.

In the sacred lotus of His navel (Tirunābhīkamala), He brought forth the entire world; having performed the creation as described in the *Tiṇṭirāl* and other texts, He fashioned the earth from the foam of the churned ocean, and became the Lord who subdues the pride of the Asuras, the one who strikes down the arrogant Tāraka, and who dwells in the sacred Kaṇṇapuram, where the gods, desiring to behold His face, long to gaze upon His eyes. He is the one who makes the hearts of the gods turn toward Him, the beloved of the goddesses. He resides in the sacred Kaṇṇapuram, which the gods seek to enter with longing.
When the Lord, who is the very essence of grace, appeared as an incarnation, he went forth, protecting even those who were wicked and hostile toward him;
he who, with his own hand, lifted up the great mountain that was the lineage of the Kuru family, which had been sinking into the mud of vice, and who, like a noble tree, provided shade for the world.
He is Caṅkaṉ Tirumarukāṉ Tācar.
Even among the Kaṅkais, you are the one who has crossed over the ocean of worldly existence; you are the nectar for those whose lineage is like a heap of impurities.
You are the one who, by the fragrance of your own family, purifies the two mountains—the mountain of the Koṅgu region and the mountain of Kaucalai—which are filled with the impurity of the Kali age.
O Śrī Kausalyā, you are the savior of your own family!

The elder brother of Śrī Janakarāja, who was eager to establish a suitable alliance with him, sent word to the King of Mithilā saying, "O King of Mithilā, the daughter of Caṇaka, known as the Great Pukal, is here!
And that elder brother was indeed the one who desired such a fitting union.

In Kaṅkāi, where the sacred bathing place is difficult to reach and the city of Karupura is far away, there is the purity found in Gaṅgaikkuḷattūr due to its occasional connection; but in Tiruppōykai, which possesses a constant and exceedingly pure relationship with Tirukkaṇṇapuram, one can easily obtain [the Lord]! He who dwells as the immortal one within our own lineage, he who is the object of enjoyment for the Kākās of the royal dynasty, he who is the beloved of Tamaraimeḷai—[I shall go] to him, my own... O Mātali, O son of Maitili! Let not those who are like the Manavāḷa forest—those greedy and lustful men—eat this sweet fruit; let them instead eat the bitter, thorny, and poisonous ones.
O Karumaṇi, even if they die, let them perish there.
Alas! They have fallen into the power of the hunter.

Having crossed over the great ocean of worldly existence, having found refuge in the land of the Supreme Lord, and being filled with the virtues of total dependence upon Him, Śrī Bharatālvān—who was thus endowed with the quality of *paratantrya*—prayed for a small portion of land.

While he was waiting there, having made a firm resolve, the Lord Himself approached him and said, "Accept me. Then, together with the Lord of the Earth (Iḷaiyaperumāḷ), he entered that forest which was teeming with various wicked creatures.

O Cakravartin Tirumakan! Even if the heroic glory of the one who wears the *cīra* (bark garment) were to perish, and even if the one who wears the *tār* (silk) were to die, you alone remain—O Lord who wears the crown that signifies supreme sovereignty, and the ring upon which the *mālaiyōṭu* (the crest-jewel) is set!
You are the one who causes all the earth to tremble under the weight of Your feet.
Even if one were to die from the bite of a venomous snake or from a fall from a mountain peak, those who have heard this [teaching] will not suffer;
for those who wear the sacred ash upon their bodies, there is no fear of death.
O Cīrāmā, you who dwell within the palm tree! May you protect us.

"Will everyone become thieves, stealing all the grain from the threshing floor? Will everyone become hunters, killing fish with nets?"—if such questions are asked, [the answer is: "I shall do everything," he said; thus, Emperumāṉār granted his grace, saying that all these activities and even all the wickednesses were merely the deceptive play (*kūṭa-pōkai*) of Iḷaiyaperumāḷ, and that all those who were enemies had become deceptive thieves.
To those who abide according to the teaching, "Even those who are wicked are indeed [his] children, and the ascetics are his very womb," [he grants his grace].

O King Arumaraṇtāna, you who said, "I would even give up my life for Arumaraṇti," you have gone to the supreme abode through your devotion to Ayōtti Nakaṟkaṭipaṭi; O Lord of the kingdom of Appaṭippaṭṭa Paṭaivīṭṭu!

The ministers said: "O King, let us go to that Kāñcīpuram; let us stay in one country for some time. Let us experience the taste of the object we seek in that particular land. Out of a longing for the object beyond that region, they went to the holy Kāñcīpuram.

Hearing the words of Śrī Kauśalyā, who was weeping and saying, "I am the mother of the one who has gone to the forest, my son, my dear child," and hearing also the words of Kaikeyī, who was speaking harshly, he [Rāma] departed from the city. O King, he has gone!
He who protected the earth with his arms like a father, he who conquered the world of the Vālis and gave it to the Rākṣasas;

O Kaṇapuram, my beloved, whose hand is adorned with jewels! O my golden jewel! *Note: This verse is from the Tamil epic *Maṇimēkalai*. It praises the heroic deeds of Rāma (the son of Daśaratha) and addresses the heroine Maṇimēkalai.*
O Mother!

When the time for my death arrived, as the hour of my departure drew near, you took me by the hand and placed me within a single house situated on the shore of the ocean; there, you granted me the grace of your presence, which enables the impossible to be accomplished, saying, "I am here with you. O Mother! You alone possess such power to bring about the inconceivable!

Did Vāli kill Rāvaṇa—who had come seeking Vāli—and thus protect the monkey race? Or did Vāli, having bound Rāvaṇa—who had come seeking Vāli and was boasting of his victory over Arai and Tuṇai—hand him over to that Great King who dwells within mountain caves, desiring to grant him the kingdom of the monkeys? O jewel, I shall grasp with my hand the gems that lie scattered here and there in this forest.
O Āli Nakarkkātippati, you who are the sustainer of the sacred Āli lineage! Having come to Vāli, you who have brought the Āli people under your command through your wisdom!
You who built the mountain fortress and protected the land of Ilankai with your intellect;
you who, by slaying the enemies, bestowed the nectar of immortality upon the gods!
When the Lord of the Kalais (the Moon) was about to set, O dear one, the fisherman Cevakan, who had built a house on the shore of the sea,
saw the mountain [Lanka] rising from the water;

having cut through the earth with his intellect and established it upon the excellent mountain within the ocean, he built Lanka by cutting away the waters and raising the land, making it firm at its very foundation!
He who churned the ocean of immeasurable depth for the sake of the gods, granting them immortality; he who, while the gods and the asuras were engaged in battle, gave the nectar to the gods!

O beloved of Kaṇṇan, whose fame is like the moon, you who are the abode of all arts and sciences—do you not reside in Tirukkaṇṇapuram so that those who desire to experience the bliss of the divine may do so?
Do you not reside there with your bow, Śrīśārṅga, which is ever victorious?
"O servant! and so forth—those who revile me, you must stand up for them, O Vīrappaṭṭai!
Even if the threshold, the door-bolt, and the key were to break, you must protect your own family; otherwise, by your own hand, you will bring shame upon the land of Maṇiḷilaṅkāi.

"O precious jewel, you who have come to this land for the sake of the *kaṇapura*—the red sandalwood, the fragrant *maruṅkal*, and the *alarum*—you who are the deliverer of the lineage of the Cakravartin kings, the one who has come to protect the kingdom...

Having spoken thus, he [bestowed] the *naṟunāṟṟattai* (the gift of the seven-thousand) upon the *uṭaiyamayirmuṭi* (the six-hundred and sixty thousand) and the *uṭaiyacakravartikulam* (the Cakravartin dynasty). He was indeed their savior.

Even if Brahmāstras and other such weapons were to fall upon me, or even if the wind were to blow against me, I would not do anything else; for to one who possesses human nature, there is no greater solace than this! Even if the waters of the Kalaini river were to flow over my head, or if the sands of that river were to be scattered upon my hands, or if the stones of that river were to pierce my feet and enter my very abode, or if the people of Tirukkaṇṇapuram were to come and embrace me—let them come to me with such intensity that they might even take my life, yet I would still say: "I need you. Thus I shall remain.

Whoever studies the *Tēvāram*, the *Acuṛaṉ*, and the *Tiruccaṟaṉkaḷ* shall become one who possesses the strength of ten elephants, who is radiant with splendor, and who is like a bee at the lotus feet of the Lord; such a person shall be adorned with gold and jewels.
Thus says Kaṇṇapparaṉ.
"O Lord,

You who created the earth, the sky, the mountains, the rivers, the trees, the forests, the cities, and all objects— beginning with the gods and asuras who are natural enemies— as well as the lands that provide space for them!

Since everyone, whether in the forest, on the mountain, or in the city, must depend upon You alone for every purpose of their creation, please come to this temple," thus did the sages pray, and He graciously consented.

Even if one does not know how to string together the Tamil garlands of speech that flow forth from the heart,
there will surely be those who will take up the pen to write the book of the Lord’s grace, which is like a stream of honey flowing from the mouth of the Lord of the Three Worlds.
In the city of Nigama,

where the daughter of Kanva was born, and in the great Tirumati, where the son of Puṭai Cūḻa was born— within that very Tirukkaṇṇapuram where Kṛṣṇa himself graced the earth with his presence— the poet Pāṭiṟṟu composed this *Cakravarti Tirumakaṉai*.

The portion beginning with "Taṉ aṭi-mēl" describes the childhood state of Cakravarti Tirumakaṉuṭai, as well as the Tamil region situated within Tirukkaṇṇapuram, which lies along the banks of the river where Śrī Kausalyā resided.

At that time, when everyone was crying out, "Who is there? Who is the master of this house? and while the sound of the *veṇkoṟṟu*—which manifests his majesty—was being raised, the venerable Kulaśekhara Perumāḷ, having heard the words of those who were about to enter, granted them the opportunity to experience the presence of both his mother and father.

These were the ones who had mastered the *Lakṣaṇas* and were thus able to discern the true nature of the one who dwells within the *Pañcapañcāśat*. They were the ones worthy of beholding his divine mother and father.

Having ruled the kingdom for sixty years, he performed all the rites for the transfer of sovereignty; indeed, in this very year, in the month of Vaḷpukaḷ, on the day of Nāraṇaṉ, having departed from this world, he fulfilled his sacred vow by declaring, "I am the servant of my dependents in every condition," and adorned the city that was fit for his sacred coronation—the city that stands as the foremost among cities. In that preeminent city... (Note: The final phrase "toḻut’ ētta" appears to be a scribal or textual corruption of "toḻuttē," meaning "standing as the foremost.")

I am the one who, having fulfilled all the duties required prior to the sacred ablution (tiru-abhiṣeka) for my father’s sake, performed the sacred ablution; I am the one who sat upon the throne while the golden palanquin (tiru-kāppu-nāṉ cātti) was being carried, remaining seated there until the time when the white elephant, adorned with its howdah, stood ready at the gate.

Thinking, "I shall go to the forest," those kings, though they had no desire to leave, set out from their respective cities. Having gone from forest to forest, they traveled for many days; emerging from one forest, they entered another, and from that forest, they went into yet another. Thus, wandering from forest to forest, they searched for him who had fled into the forest.
While they were thus searching, crying out, "Where are you? Where are you? and looking about in distress, they saw him fleeing toward Mount Umā.

O Śrī Kausalyā, daughter of Kaṇṇai! You who have raised us—who were like a thorny forest that swallowed us—having made us grow up; you who, when our family was sinking into the ocean of misery, lifted us up by the hair, lifting us from the mire of sorrow and grief, and lifting us even from the depths of despair—you alone are our savior!

The heroes who could not endure even a slight blow have now fled far away, leaving behind their wives who weep with grief; even those who once lived there have gone to the distant mountains, abandoning both their great wealth and their noble lineage!
My mind is consumed by the fire of my own valor, and my heart is pierced by the arrows of my weapons—both the great and the small;
alas, my heart is tormented! Above the clouds, from the very source of the waters that flow through all time, the water falls.

Whether it be a cloth from Piṟaku, Piṉpu, or Piṟakuvāli, they will say, "I have come for this"; and whether it be from Piṉṉai or Kaṇmaṟai, they will say, "I have come for this."

"O Mother! I am here, dwelling in this land that nourishes my life. Thus she spoke, and her mother embraced her.

Then, as they conversed with overflowing love, saying, "O daughter, how wonderful it is that you have come from afar," she took her own daughter—who was adorned with ornaments, whose sacred breasts were swelling, who possessed a deep voice, and who was like a single essence—into her lap and embraced her most fervently. O Daughter, embrace me; embrace me as my very being, for you are my life-breath. Thus she spoke, and they wept together.

then,
as if to see the face of the one who moves with the gait of a rutting elephant, the lotus opens its eyes, and the *tāmarai* flower, longing to behold his divine countenance, blooms.

When my mother-in-law scolds me, saying, "My son-in-law does not work; he stays at home all day long," and when she speaks thus while I am sitting on the ground floor of her house, what can I do? Even if I were to weave baskets, mats, and hampers, and carry them out to sell in the market, it would be of no avail. I am like a flower, a herb, a creeper, a vine, or a young plant that has withered away.
When the king of Kāmaṇṛpa saw me, he was struck with wonder; he asked, "Who are you?
and as I stood there, he said, "I am the son of that man who built this palace. Then, having heard my words, he spoke to me: "Come, let us go to the city of Cēral.
Thus, I set out from there toward the land of the Chēra king.

The jasmine flowers and the *kuñci* blossoms, having gathered together, fill the air with their fragrance; the sacred mountain slopes are covered in lush greenery. For the sake of men, the Lord, whose feet are like the rising sun, shines forth from his golden crown, casting a thousand rays of light upon the sacred mountain ranges. In this sacred forest where every tree bears fruit, amidst the divine play, he who was born from a clump of reeds—Viśvāmitra—was struck by the arrow of the hunter and brought down.

"O Mother! Why do you bring these artificial ornaments—these marks of the brush and collyrium—to adorn my natural locks? My son, who has performed his ablutions, has become free from passion after eating the thousand varieties of food served by the sixteen thousand maidens; he is now ready to depart. But as for that delicate prince, who is worthy of such luxuries, how can I bear to let him go? Thus spoke the mother.
"O Brahmins who dwell in Ayodhyā, saying 'The King is indeed our master'—is that dharma?

Speak, O Sumantra, who knows the royal duties and has traveled through the waters of the world! Speak, O venerable Śrī Vasiṣṭha, the preceptor of this lineage, who has instructed us in the duties of kingship!
Let gold be brought, and let the son and his mother be brought forth! Thus he spoke.
If my husband dies, I shall die by jumping into the fire;
if my son dies, I shall die by leaping from the top of the palace roof;
if you abandon me, I shall die by drowning myself in the sea—having made such a vow, I remain here, awaiting death, within these two rooms.

The preceptors, who lived saying "Blessed indeed is he who has sons and a wife," remained there and taught all the Vedas and Śāstras; they also taught the Lord who dwelt there, as well as the wives of those who studied them. They taught me, their own daughter-in-law, how to weave the cloth for the morning libation, how to prepare the sacrificial fire, and how to perform the rituals of the ancestors. Furthermore, they taught me, who was of a gentle nature, my duties toward my mother-in-law and my husband.
Having fled into the forest, you have abandoned your father;

having fled into the forest, you have abandoned your son, who was dearer to you than your own life; and having fled into the forest, you have abandoned both Perumāḷ and Iḷaiya-Perumāḷ, saying, "I am not their father. Having committed these acts—treachery against your brother and the abandonment of me—you say, "What is the purpose of your coming here?
What is the purpose of your coming here? You have done all this; what is the purpose of your coming here?

O you who dwell in this world, enjoying the pleasures of worldly existence—both sons and husbands—having built a house for yourselves, listen: if your son Perumāḷ were to fall into a pit, would I not likewise fall into heaven? Therefore, you must experience the pleasures of this world while they still remain! For one day, when the tree withers and the leaves fall, he will surely come and take away both your wealth and your affection, as well as your very life. Go, then, and gather them all together today!
Having taken both me and my word as proof, if you say that I have indeed gone to the forest,
then let my father strike me with a hundred arrows; yet, having endured that for one day,
I shall take up my bow and arrows, and in a single moment, I shall seize the divine Śārṅga bow from the hand of Śrī Paraśurāma.

May that Lord, who—having attained the other world through the power of the penance he had accumulated by enduring the harshness of the forest for your sake—departed after leaving behind his mountain, his affection, and his renown; and who, likewise, endured the calamity of Queen Kausalyā as she lamented, "O Rāma! while clutching the mountain that had been given to her as a token of affection by me with great austerity, and who was weeping as she held it to her bosom.

Having taken both me and my word as true, you went away; yet, having cast aside that bond of affection which existed between us, you have now come back and said, "I am your father. O King! Having held me in your heart for three days, proclaiming the truth, why do you now act so deceitfully, making my falsehood appear as truth? Why do you speak thus, O Lord?

O Mother, even if you were to cry out "Mother! for every single step until the end of many births, and even if those passing births were to pass away, I shall surely remain as a son to you; this is my firm resolve.
Even if you were to cry out until the end of the world, I am not one who would break the bond of affection that protects those under my care;
I am one whose heart is filled with love! Therefore, do not let your face wither, nor your hair turn gray, nor your eyes become clouded with grief.

Having measured out the earth with my strides, I bound it with my strides; then, having entered the golden city, you were fleeing in terror, and as you fled through the city, I too was fleeing in terror.
When I asked, "Where are you going?", they said, "The sons of Manu have come.
Then the sons of Manu struck them down.

and having heard the account of how they were about to leap into the fire with their eyes fixed on the forest, she became distressed by the report concerning Kaikeyī herself.

"O Kāṇaka, I am going to Mithilā; you go to Nākara. You have come here seeking me, saying, 'I am searching for him who is wandering about as a mendicant for the sake of anyone. Having thus spoken, I too am going to Mithilā, having set out from Ayodhyā, which is adorned for the holy consecration (*tiru-abhiṣeka*).
You are staying in that city where you were born; I am going to that city where you dwell, even though it is like heaven itself.
O descendant of Manu, you are indeed born of the lineage of Manu."
When Rāma came to this forest,
he who was the protector of those who sought refuge,

he who was the beloved of his subjects, he who was the hero of the Kōḷiyas, and he who was the son of the great Kulaśekhara, he, the King of the Colas, built a fortress on the shore that he had reached.

Whether it be a garland of rags, a Tamil garland, or a garland of flowers—whether he appears as one who has entered into the Vedas or as one who has emerged from them, and so forth—in every such manner, the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of All and the Most Exalted, having descended into the womb of another being subject to karma, remains untouched by that karma; this is the meaning of the verse beginning with "takāta kāṭṭil pukkāṉ. This is the essence of the matter.

"O Tārā! O Ārnta! and so forth—having ruled for eighteen thousand years, when the kingdom was being destroyed by the Mālai [mountain] tribes, he who crossed the mountains and rose up as a Cakravartin, the one who spoke thus:

"O Kūr! Those who dwell on the other side [of the shore] have turned their minds away from the Lord and become intent upon sense-objects.

The Introduction: Having lived for time immemorial in this world, she has now come to experience the childhood exploits of Kṛṣṇa, whom Devakī bore as her son. While living here, she has tasted the milk of the cowherd settlement; she has experienced the sweet words spoken by Śrī Kauśalā in the midst of the people.

Having experienced everything during his childhood stage, when he reached youth, it was not necessary for him to experience [it] again; because the universal sovereignty that had been obtained by his father was already present, he attained it simply by being born, and thus he discarded that [need] as soon as he was born.

In the *Tirumoḷi*, it is said: "All the lands that have appeared on earth are but the shores; in the sacred city of Tiruccitrakūṭam, where the Lord of the Cakravartin dwells eternally, the Blessed Śrī Vālmīki took his incarnation and, having personally experienced the accounts of those incarnations, perceives them all simultaneously through the clarity of his son's wisdom. This is the meaning: that he possesses a mind so vast that it is like the ocean, and a memory so sharp it is like a lamp that never flickers.
When the lamp of the Kula lineage was extinguished, the hero who emerged from it and protected it with his own life was Rāma;

he whose face is kind toward his own kin, he who dwells on Mount Citrakūṭa, he who is the very essence of his own people—thus shall we gaze upon him, the Lord, as he emerges from the forest. May that day come!

The introductory verses (*avatārikai*) and the *pāṭṭu*: Having fulfilled the purpose of all the gods, the Lord manifested His divine incarnation (*tiru-avatāram*). Having brought forth the objects of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the places of enjoyment, He established Ayodhyā, which was built upon the very thought of Him who fills the entire expanse of space. It is called by the names Ayodhyā and Aparājitā; it is the supreme abode (*paramapada*), a city that is invincible to enemies.
If one asks, "Who are those who have gone to this supreme abode and dwell there?"— it is not merely a dwelling famous throughout all the worlds,

but a city adorned with ornaments that shines like a lamp illuminating the entire earth; and it is a place where even all the worlds, by means of their own splendor, proclaim "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Light," and wherein that Supreme Light itself dwells.

In the lineage of that Sun, who dispelled all the darkness from the world—saying "Who is he?"—there arose a hero whose splendor was peerless, like a second sun; by his own heroic qualities, he restored the race of the gods to life when they had perished.

Rāma, who possesses the lotus-eyed nature characterized by universal sovereignty—the banner of protection raised over the world when the divine race was threatened by the wicked—was one who bore on his forehead the beauty of the dark cloud that arose from the ocean, as well as the splendor of the Śeṣa-serpent coiled upon the earth; he was one whose locks of hair were beautiful both in their natural state and when adorned with ornaments, and who could distinguish between favorable and unfavorable circumstances even while playing at dice. That he was called "Vīra" (the Hero) in the battle was appropriate for his lineage, just as [the name] Satya [is appropriate].

On the shore of Tillai-nagar, Tiruccitrakūṭam, which is present for us to experience simultaneously with that incarnation, there exists one who is ever-present and near to all those living in future times; He who grants life to us so that we may experience Him face-to-face at that time— He is the Lord Himself,
the Śeṣin, whom the Lord has designated as His own.

Introduction—First Act. Having slain all the Rākṣasas who had come forth, and having fulfilled the desire of the sages by exterminating them, he set out to destroy Tāḍakā and her kin.
Having seized that Tāḍakā who had emerged, he encountered another Tāḍakā; there was no end to her deceit. There was no end to her wickedness, O Tāḍakā!
Piercing his chest with his claws, the Great Lord (Śiva) went forth, his eyes wide open, as if to consume the mountain of his own heart. He went forth, burning away [all things].

Having performed the *varu-kuruti* (the ritual of pouring water) and the *poḷi-tara-cempāṭṭu*, he went toward the mountain on the shore; blood flowed from his body as he struck it with his hand, yet he did not feel even a slight pain. He recited the sacred *mantra* and danced, while the sage Mārkaṇḍeya, who was fearless and had mastered the Vedas, repeatedly praised him. Having thus completed all the prescribed rites for his own sake, he prepared to perform the sacrifice.

The sons of Mārīca and Subāhu, who were obstacles to the sacrifice and had taken the lives of the sages, were struck down and killed by him. "Is Mārīca dead? he asked. "He is lying here, half-dead," they replied.

Then, in that land adorned with the spring season—which was beautiful to behold, refreshing to the weary, and decorated with blossoming flowers that grew in the cool shade of trees and bloomed in the sunlight—the three thousand Brāhmaṇas, who had no other purpose in life, arrived. Three thousand of them came forward.

With their faces turned toward him, their eyes fixed upon him, and their hearts captivated by his beauty, they stood with palms joined in reverence, offering their devotion. They spoke thus: "O King, you who are ever victorious, whose splendor is like that of the rising sun, and who are the very essence of the world! They praised him, their speech flowing like a river of nectar.

Having heard that the city of Tiruchitrakūṭam was being besieged by the army of the Pāṇḍya king— who had come out from the forest with his troops,
having set fire to the dry wood and grass, and who was raining down arrows like thunderbolts upon the city— Kulasekhara,
whose valor was as firm as a mountain peak, went forth from the city to meet the enemy. He then entered Tiruchitrakūṭam, which lay within his own domain.
Even with this much, the two-eyed one (Kāṇa) who was born from the ear of Kaṇ—the one who brought forth the earth—was unable to reach the end of the ocean;

and Kāṇapeṟṟa, having gathered the two lands, was unable to reach the end of the ocean; and Imayavan, having gathered the three lands, was unable to reach the end of the ocean; and Nērōvvār, having gathered the four lands, was unable to reach the end of the ocean; and Tāmē, having gathered the five lands, was unable to reach the end of the ocean; and Alarkottu, having gathered the six lands, was unable to reach the end of the ocean; and Alarukira Pukkaḷai, having gathered the seven lands, was unable to reach the end of the ocean; and Uṭaiya Curuṇṭu, having gathered the eight lands, was unable to reach the end of the ocean; and Uṭaiya Kaikeyi, having gathered the nine lands, was unable to reach the end of the ocean; and then even his own father, Aḻakālu, having gathered the ten lands, became a wandering beggar, crying out, "O Cakravartin! and begging for alms.

"O son! Kaikeyī is standing right here, having come from Cakravarti-vāy. Your mothers have gone away, having set out for Kāṭṭēṟa-pōka,"—by these words spoken by Kaikeyī, the prince was so overwhelmed with grief that he could not bear it. "I am renouncing this kingdom that has come down through my family lineage! he cried, and without even waiting for the arrival of those who had come to fetch him, saying "Let them go," he threw his own body into the Gaṅgā at Tuṟai-kaṅkāi.

When he had crossed the river Kukkan Kaṭattu, he was met with affection by the people of Tampimārai; they welcomed him with great devotion, holding up their hands in reverence. Thinking that the Lord might have come to see Niṉṟavaṉu, Śrī Bharatāḻvār and Śrī Guha Perumāḷ—who had been deceived by the ruse—set out for the forest on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Having crossed the river, they proceeded through a forest inhabited by wicked beasts where human traffic was absent.

To those who dwell in Tiruchchittirakūṭam, contemplating the beauty of the mountain that stands as a refuge for others, let them behold with their own eyes that very same splendor shining upon Citrakūṭa; let them behold with their own eyes that very same Lord who dwells there at all times, available for experience by everyone, and let them behold with their own eyes Him who is ever-present, even as they go about their work. Let them behold Him with their own eyes, and let them go forth to experience Him.
In this land, praised as the most excellent among all countries where the Lord has graciously descended, there dwell those who possess wisdom;

these are the ever-seeing ones, the eternal sages who abide in their true nature—these are the Ālvārs. Even though they have renounced everything and cast aside their very selves, they remain intent only on the pilgrimage [to the Lord].
