The forest of his fame spread through the four quarters; he pierced the vital organs of his enemies with sharp arrows, and having slain their pride, he took their lives.
Having conquered Tiruccitrakūṭa, he seized its wealth and, crossing the sea, he subdued the other lands, making them pay tribute. It was he alone who did this.
The forest-dwellers were terrified when the army advanced; they encountered Virādha, who had come from the mountains with his followers.

Then, having seen Agastya, whom the sage Agastya himself had granted a vision, Śūrpaṇakhī—who was like a thorn to the forest-dwellers, a thorn to the arts, and a thorn that pierced the very core of the arts—was struck down by the arrow of the Sage.
Thus ends the third canto.

When Khara and Dūṣaṇa, having seen the beauty and deformity of the one who had come to kill them, pierced his vital organs with their sharp arrows and struck him down, they were filled with grief and lamented.

Then, impelled by Rāvaṇa, Mārīca—who had come disguised as a magical deer—was killed; and when [Rāma] returned, he saw that the entire forest, including the trees and the ground, was covered in blood. Thus, having observed all these signs, he understood the purpose behind the presence of water on the shore and the presence of wind, and he concluded that the one who had crossed over must be there.
The sun having risen, the rays of light spread across the sky; by the grace of fortune, the earth became a place for their movement.
Having crossed the desert sands of the body, they reached Vaikuṇṭha, the forest of the beloved;
there, the sage Aruṇan Kātal, having attained the state of a bee, remained in the lotus of the Goddess’s face, while the lords of the city of Ilankai were like bees at her feet.
Having sent the wind-god Hanuman to search for her, Rama, who was weeping as he searched for his mother who had entered the fire at Mount Citrakuta, has now come here seeking me.
Alas! Alas! I am lost! I am lost!

The great Takshaka, out of pride in his lineage and the splendor of his city Alakā, challenged the Lord to a game of dice; the Lord accepted the challenge, and Rāvaṇa, having entered into that gambling match, lost his life and was sent to the supreme abode by the Great Mother. Thus, it is said that the Fortune of Viṣṇu is his own daughter, while the wealth of the Lord is merely the stakes in the game of dice.

While Sugriva was dwelling in the forest, having taken refuge with affection under the protection of Vali—who was like a king to the deer that lived there, grazing on the grass and gazing at the trees—the Lord of the Rakshasas, Ravana, remained deluded by the pride and arrogance of thinking himself the master of Lanka, the city of Ilankai, and the subduer of Vali, who possessed exceeding strength and valor; yet, he shattered that pride and arrogance, and having bestowed his grace upon Vali, he cut him down.

In times such as the *tillai* festival, when people experience [the Lord] in various ways, I too am there; yet, for the sake of the Universal Sovereign (*Sarveśvara*), the Lord who is eternally present here, I have come to offer my own body at His sacred feet. Even though He is difficult to attain, they have come to Him with such great ease (*saulabhya*). Having crossed the deep waters of the *kurai*, *kaṭalai*, *aṭal*, and *ampāl* rivers, having bound their hair and crossed the *kulai*, they have come on foot, having themselves carried me across.
The king who protects Eri, Neṭum, Vēl, Arakkaroṭu, and Ilankai—having taken his life and having seen him, he shall rule; now, having entered Tirumakaḷōṭu, the hero shall dwell there.
He who rules Tillainakara and Tiruccitrakūṭa, ruling over his own land, shall rule with great splendor;
the enemy’s army shall flee, and where else can the enemy go? Only I shall oppose that very army!

The enemy host rose up against me; thinking, "What shall I do? I stood firm, my mind wavering. Then, with a great roar, I built a rampart of four walls and, leaping over them, I quickly seized the enemy in my arms.
I said, "I will carry you across my chest," and placing the mountains upon my shoulders, I quickly turned back and set out toward the end of the earth.

At that time, when he was about to kill his enemies with his arrows, Rāvaṇa, the lord of Laṅkā, who had risen up in the city of the Rakṣasas, took away his life-breath, gave him his kingdom, and bestowed upon him the sovereignty that had been granted by the gods, which was difficult to attain and which caused all those who saw it to tremble with fear. It was he himself.

Having acquired the kingdom beginning with Tillai-nagar, he ruled over the realm where the sacred footprints were clearly manifest; protecting the sovereignty of that kingdom with his own independent power, he was indeed a king among kings. He who was called Araci, Akattiyan, and Vāy—who, having heard the words "I shall give gold, gems, and pearls," went forth with his great army, struck down the enemy, and brought back the children who had fled to the sacred forest—was a man of great renown.
Having heard the life stories of that Lord who dwells on the shore of the Pārvati river at Tillainagar Tiruccitrakūṭam,
we shall go to hear those very deeds performed by our own Lord. With this resolve,

we shall go to the auspicious city of Ayodhyā— which is adorned for his golden consecration, which is beautiful to behold, and which is filled with elephants caparisoned with fine jewels— to see the entire world bowing down and crying out in joy as he emerges from the waters.

Having regained his kingdom in Ayodhyā and ruling over the entire world, King Daśaratha, who was free from any further duties, heard the account of the past concerning Rāvaṇa— who had previously been killed by Agastya Bhagavān after being subdued by the sage’s curse— and having received this request, he granted leave for the composition of the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*, which describes the history of his own son, the illustrious Janaka, who restored the earth to its former state, and of Kuśa and Lava, who were born to him. Thus, [the sage] began the work.

We, who have come here to Tiruccitrakūṭam to experience with all our senses the story of my beloved Lord—who dwells there eternally—have attained a state of mind that experiences the nectar of the divine race as if it were a single moment. Having seen your Campaka tree, which has grown tall and beautiful, and having tasted its sweet fruit, we have now reached this shore; yet, though we have obtained the jewel of this life, we must still cross over the salt water by clinging to the boat of your fame. Having reunited the life of the Brahmin son of Uttaṅka, who had died while crossing the river Ceḷuṃ, and having graciously bestowed upon him a necklace of pearls as large as the mountain Agastya, Śrī Śatrughnāḻvār entered the city of Ayodhyā, slew the demon Lavaṇāsura, and caused him to dwell in the world of heroes.

Due to the curse of the sage Dūrvāsas, as mentioned in the *Muṇivaṉ* and other texts, my second inner self (the subtle body) departed for the presence of the Lord of the Earth (Raṅganātha), who is his very life-breath. Having left behind that body which had become a mere heap of flesh and bone, he took up his eternal residence on the shore at Tiruccitrakūṭam. That state of being easily accessible—wherein we may experience that Supreme Lord by constantly contemplating Him with unceasing devotion—is no longer present here today.
Then, having entered Vaikuṇṭha with the moving and unmoving beings, he ascended the mountain of his own body,
which was like a jewel upon the earth; there, amidst the sounds of the *ilangu*, *maṇi*, *neṭum*, *tōl*,
*nāṅku*, *tōṉṟa*, *viṇ*, *muḷutuṃ*, and *etir*, he embraced his mother, who had come forth from her own body, and led her to Tiruccitrakūṭa, the city of his own abode.
Thus, as he went along day after day crying out, "Where is he? Where is he?", for three days there was neither food nor drink;

even the trees withered, as expressed by the contrast [in the verse]: "Even the plants and trees withered" (*api vṛkṣāḥ parimlānāḥ*). By the grace of his presence, it was revealed that not even the slightest breath was seen in Ayodhyā, and all others, even those born of animal wombs, remained devoted to Rāma—thus it is said. Then Ilaiyaperumāḷ departed for the supreme abode.

Having struck down the great serpent-king, the natural-born enemy of serpents, with his eightfold roar; having caused the four divine arrows—those which possess the marks of the end of the host of Asuras and which blaze with heroic glory—to fall upon them; and having cast them into the supreme abode, he is the Lord who has swallowed all his own flesh.

In the verse beginning with "Tillai na kaṟ" (Tiruvāymoḻi 10.10.1), the one who possesses the knowledge of time (*kālatattva*) teaches that He dwells eternally here within us. You all, having no other purpose, take refuge in Him and become fulfilled. In Tillai, in the city of Tiruccitrakūṭam, while the son of the Wind-god (Hanumān) was leaping across the ocean, he covered the entire expanse; then his father [Vāyu] emerged from beneath the waters and, up until that moment, carried away his own realm.

Even those who know the *kol* [the *Tolkāppiyam*] do not know the *paṭai* [the *Eṭṭuttokai*]; even those who know the *koṟṟam* [the *Poruḷatikāram*] do not know the *vāḷ* [the *Kural*]. Who among the *kōḷiyar* [the learned] has ever composed a work that is both *kuṭai* [profound] and *kulacēkaram* [pure]?

Is there anyone who has composed a *tamil* *mālai* [poetic string] that is both *nal* [correct] and *inal* [unblemished]? Is there anyone who has mastered the *tikaḻ* [the *Nāṉārūpattal*] and the *nāraṇaṉ* [the *Tirukkural*], and who, having mastered them, has become a master of the *nigama* [the sacred tradition]? No one at all.

In the verse beginning with *tillai naṅkar*, the Lord has declared that His nature does not go elsewhere; thus, having taken up residence in this sacred Tiruvaṭiyai, He makes it His eternal abode. To the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) who possesses manifold virtues—such as being praised in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa* with words like "He dwells in all lands" (*ellai il cīr*)—and to the story of Śrī Rāma which tells how his father chose him over the elder brother to ascend to the supreme state (*paramapada*), he offers praise: "The one who, at the time when the dawn rose from the ocean that had swallowed the earth, protected the land and its people. Thus, he sings the praises of Him who is the King of Kings.
To the fisherman Veṟṟiyai and his wife Aḷaki, [the Lord] granted the village of Uṭaiyavāḷ.

To the fisherman Kōṉ, [He granted] Kōṉkōḷi—[that is,] Uṟaiyūr. This was granted by Śrīkulaśekhara Perumāḷ, who was pleased with Kuṭai Kulacēkaraṉ, the son of Rājāāṉavar, who served the Cōḻa king in Veṇkoṟṟakuṭai. It was issued by the grace of [the Lord].
Who will compose the Tamil garland for Nal? Who will compose the Tamil garland for this land that has risen up?
Nala, Tikal, Narana, Aṭikīl, and Nannuvārē—those who have reached the supreme abode, the lords of all, are singing the praises of the Lord’s sacred feet.
